Mr. Speaker, negotiations for a trade agreement between Canada and the U.S.S.R. have now reached a stage where a basis for agreement has been established. speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: EAST GERMANY-STATEMENT CORRECTING NEWS REPORT RESPECTING REFUGEE FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is important that I correct an erroneous news report which was prominently displayed in virtually all newspapers and broadcast several times over the radio in the Federal Republic of Germany yesterday to the effect that German farmers who have recently fled from the Soviet zone cannot emigrate immediately to Canada.
This statement is contrary to fact, since our officers in West Germany deal without delay with the applications of persons who have fled from the east zone of Germany and who have been classified as refugees by the authorities of the federal republic.
It is a matter of record that Canada has accepted many thousands of refugees from Germany. It would be most unfortunate if this erroneous news report should act as a deterrent to the movement of agriculturists from East Germany, who are welcome in Canada and for whom excellent settlement opportunities continue to exist.

speakerposition: stagedirection

subtopic: STATEMENT ON VISIT BY MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask either the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Labour whether they will be in a position soon to make a report on their week end at Elliot Lake.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT ON VISIT BY MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could report briefly now.
The Minister of Labour and I visited Elliot Lake on Saturday and Sunday. We were exceptionally well received by the people of that area, had a long conference with representatives of the various organizations in town who presented half a dozen briefs to us in the course of Saturday afternoon, drove round the community and saw the dwellings there, the schools and the hospital, and met ever so many people. We reviewed the situation generally, and are taking into consideration the suggestions made by the citizens of Elliot Lake with regard to the present situation there and the future.
The problem requires action on a broad front, and that action is going forward. In the first place the citizens themselves have shown commendable initiative in organizing the community with the intention of attracting to that area industry from other parts, and in generally looking after the welfare of those who are disturbed because of the employment situation. The mining companies are taking an active interest in the situation and are endeavouring on their own account to make plans for maintaining employment in the area, and increasing it similarly by encouraging other industry.
The provincial government of Ontario have indicated in the legislature their very keen interest in the welfare of Elliot Lake and are similarly making plans to assist. The dominion government is also considering ways and means of coming to the assistance of a community which through no fault of its own is facing circumstances which for some
Inquiries of the Ministry of the people there are rather trying, to say the least. I think it will be possible within a very short interval to provide from our sources-that is from the dominion government-some assistance to Elliot Lake, and the other organizations I have mentioned will also be doing something very soon.
It is a model community situated in the northern part of this province. It represents the type of effort that is being made in developing northern parts of Canada through the mining industry, and it has great possibilities for the future. It is recognized that the uranium industry is now suffering a contraction, but the evidence that can be produced by experts in the field indicates that within a few years the demand for uranium may again increase and, that being so, there will be a good future for the industry in Elliot Lake and in other areas that produce uranium. Unfortunately there is at present a time lag between the period of 1963 or 1965 and 1970, and in that interval certain things will have to be done to sustain the community.
There is no doubt whatever that the government is keenly aware of the problems affecting the people of Elliot Lake and is anxious to do everything that is reasonably possible to meet that situation. In my opinion the people of Elliot Lake are showing great initiative and remarkable courage under trying conditions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, April 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Benidickson.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Cenfre):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the ten o'clock adjournment last night I had congratulated the Minister of Finance for a budget job well done. I had pointed out that this year's balanced budget would bolster confidence in Canada's economy. I referred to a chart which graphically indicated the country's financial growth, showing an increase in the gross national product to a record $34.5 billion in 1959. I said this tremendous growth was due to this government's policy and to the long term planning and tenacity of the Minister of Finance.
I drew attention to the great increase in federal contributions to the provincial governments since the present Minister of Finance assumed office. Unconditional payments, conditional payments and special payments to the provincial governments will total $1,300,900,000 this fiscal year compared with about half that amount, $689,400,000, paid in 1956-57, the last fiscal year of the Liberal government.
In connection with these federal contributions to the provinces, I would like to continue with an assessment of what Ottawa is paying to the Saskatchewan government under these arrangements. I have here a break-down of these federal payments to the Saskatchewan government for the 1960-61 fiscal

year showing a comparison with what the Liberal government paid in the last fiscal year during which it was in office, 1956-57. Unconditional grants to the Saskatchewan government this year will total $43,068,000 compared with $29,562,000 in 1956-57. Conditional grants to Saskatchewan will total $27,894,000 compared with $7,723,000 in the last fiscal year of the Liberal government. Nearly $71 million is being paid to the Saskatchewan government this year by way of conditional and unconditional grants, compared with $37,285,000 paid by the Liberal government in 1956-57.
Saskatchewan will receive nearly $41 million this year from tax rental and equalization payments, compared with $27,432,000 in 1956-57. The equalization payments are designed to pay to the provinces the difference between the tax rental payments per capita to the provinces of Ontario and British Columbia and the tax rental payments per capita to each of the other provinces. In the case of Saskatchewan this difference for 196061 is estimated at $24.76 per capita, which means that $22,680,000 will be paid to Saskatchewan under this agreement.
In connection with this greater federal payment to the provincial governments the mayor of Saskatoon recently made a very interesting comment, as reported in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. He said:
Saskatchewan municipalities are in urgent need of more financial assistance from the provincial government to ease the increasing burden of municipal taxes. He hoped that the Saskatchewan government would share the increase in tax rentals from Ottawa.
The Saskatchewan mayor is reported in the newspaper to have said:
The Saskatchewan provincial government might be able to claim a reduced provincial debt, but the debt reduction was due to a shift in the tax load from the provincial to the municipal governments.
Earlier in my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I referred to the fact that the great industry of agriculture, like all other economic groups, will benefit at least indirectly from sound government financing and a balanced budget. This government has provided many benefits to agriculture, and there will be a great many other farm benefits arising from the government's long term agricultural policy. In the course of a speech in this house the Liberal member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) made a very interesting comment on this government's farm price policy. Here is what he said as reported at page 2464 of Hansard of Friday, March 25. I shall read the translation. He was referring to the supplementary estimates brought in by the Minister of Agriculture, and he said:
Under this item, we are asked to vote an amount of $57,661,176 under the heading "Operating Loss
The Budget-Mr. Pascoe Sustained by the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Board." That, Mr. Chairman, is the highest amount Canada has ever spent to support farm prices, since the passing of the Agricultural Prices Support Act in 1946.
If we look at the report, we find that the total amount spent under the act since 1946 is approximately $100 million, including the losses arising from the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, mainly in the western provinces, and which accounted for $70 million on that amount.
Under the Liberal administration, from 1946 to March 1957, the Agricultural Prices Support Act cost $25,052,806.98.
Now if you look at the expenditures for the past three years, that is since the Conservative government took over you find that in 1958, Canada spent close to $6 million, and in 1959, $15,124,000. Now, for the year 1959-60, we are asked to vote $57,661,176.
That means that since the election of the Conservative government, it has cost the taxpayers the substantial amount of $78,773,819 to support agricultural prices.
In short, therefore, it can be said that in the last 12 years of Liberal administration, it cost us $25 million to support those prices, while in three years of Conservative administration, the amount expended was $78 million.

speechtext:
Coming from a prairie farm region and an area principally devoted to grain raising, I naturally consider that bolstering the position of the western wheat farmer is one of the main problems facing this government. It is not a problem of this government's making; it is a problem that has been building up for years. The Leader of the Opposition made this clear when he said, according to a report in the Edmonton Journal of October 3, 1958, that agriculture had not had a fair share of the national income for the past 10 or 15 years.
This government's long range farm policy, Mr. Speaker, is the first real attempt at a national agricultural policy. Its full impact may not be felt for some time. That is why I believe some action of a more immediate nature should be taken this session to ease the problems of particular groups, such as the western wheat farmers. I use the term "immediate action" to differentiate between it and the long range farm program.
First I want to deal with this long range program. I know I am not making an original statement when I say that farming, which once was regarded as a somewhat individual way of life, has now become a business proposition, with all the problems of high cost operations and also with at least some of the

The Budget-Mr. Pascoe hopes of the financial returns offered in business. When I say farming is now a business proposition I do not mean that farms must necessarily become big farms. Personally I believe in the preservation of family farms that can become economic units. Such family farms were the backbone of the economy in Saskatchewan in earlier days, and I am hoping the federal government policies will help to maintain these family farms in the years to come.
In the government's long range farm policy there are three main points of attack on present problems, and here I speak as a western farmer of the problems of western grain farmers. The first point is more adequate long term credit to help put farms on the necessary business basis. The second is a guarantee of a minimum yearly grain income through crop insurance, worked out in cooperation with provincial governments. The third is continuing efforts, through the Canadian wheat board, to sell more wheat both on the export and on the domestic markets. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to hear the announcement by the Prime Minister of the trade agreement with Soviet Russia, which will take more of our wheat.
Great interest is now centred on this government's long term credit plans, especially among young farmers and among those who would like to be farmers. It is almost impossible today for a young man to start on a farm without sufficient credit, or for older farmers to expand or reorganize their operations without such credit. In commenting on this situation an editorial in the Family Herald of March 12, 1959 had this to say:
Credit is essential. The problem Is to learn how to use it as a tool, and to lessen the risk. There was a day when the necessity of borrowing was thought to be the last mark of disaster for a farmer; when keeping out of debt was a mark of honour. Since then, farmers have learned that credit is a tool that may be as helpful to them as any other tool. Farming, besides being a way of life, is an industry and a business, and it must operate as such. The wise use of credit is just one of the business skills that farming requires. And a hearty welcome awaits any sound scheme that will make credit easier to get.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that under this government's new policy we certainly have made more credit available to farmers. This government believes it has worked out a sound farm credit program that will operate under the Department of Agriculture and help young farmers, through some form of supervision, to see that credit is used in the best way possible. The 47 prairie members on the government side can take some credit -if I may use the term in another sense-


for this new credit plan, especially for keeping the interest rate at 5 per cent. The 5 per cent interest rate is quite a contrast to the interest rate of 63, per cent charged under the farm credit plan for young farmers set up recently by the Saskatchewan government.
The second part of this government's long range farm program, a crop insurance plan, would guarantee a minimum level of annual grain income and would fit in with the credit program. The Saskatchewan government at first rejected the crop insurance program as an insult. That was the word used. Now it has changed its mind, possibly because of pressure from farmers and farm groups, and is going to follow the lead of the Manitoba government and set up test areas to see how crop insurance can be worked out. The federal government will pay one half the cost of administration and 20 per cent of the insurance premiums. This is the same rate of contribution that is made by the government to the unemployment insurance fund. I emphasize this point, Mr. Speaker. Unemployment insurance contributions from the federal government are in practically the same proportion as has been agreed to for crop insurance.
On the third front of the government's farm policy, aggressive action to sell more wheat, the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave the house an outline of what has been accomplished. It was a good report, despite the attempts of the opposition to minimize the export figures. Canada has held her position as the world's leading exporter of wheat in commercial markets, with cash sales in the last crop year exceeding the cash sales of United States wheat by 125 million bushels. In this crop year Canadian wheat exports have been running about 10 million bushels ahead of last year. I have a chart here which shows that situation. It indicates an increase each month over the same month last year. Increased world production of wheat, continued restrictive measures in some countries and the pressure in other countries to dispose of wheat surpluses are obstacles to greater wheat board sales; but, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce points out, the high quality of Canadian wheat is the chief sustaining feature of our world trade.
These three points have been mentioned in the house on other occasions, Mr. Speaker, but I make no apologies for outlining them again. They contain the three essentials of an integrated farm program of particular interest to the prairie; namely, more adequate credit facilities to establish farms on a business basis, some assurance of annual income through crop insurance, and continuing efforts to sell more wheat.

It is recognized that this is a long range policy and that its benefits may not be fully felt for some years. Saskatchewan members have suggested on other occasions, and I take this opportunity to suggest it again, that help of a more immediate nature could be given prairie wheat farmers through a two-price system for wheat sales. A two-price system would mean that wheat sold on the domestic market for human consumption, at present about 50 million bushels, would be sold at a price higher than the price on the world market and more in line with other Canadian prices.
If the 50 million bushels of wheat for domestic consumption sold for $1 a bushel above the export market price, this would mean an extra $50 million for distribution to grain growers through the Canadian wheat board. It is my personal view that under such a plan the additional money could be distributed on either a limited acreage basis or on the basis of a limited number of bushels for each farmer, say on the first 2,000 bushels delivered by any one farmer. Under this arrangement the smaller farmers would receive a good share of the additional money.
In connection with the domestic market for wheat, I want to refer to the decreasing consumption of bread. Based on its nutritional value, bread is one of our cheapest foods. In view of this is it surprising that in Canada, where we grow the best milling wheat, the per capita consumption of bread is going down. As a farmer and the member for the constituency of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, where probably the best bread-making wheat in the world is grown, I am disturbed over this situation and consider that something should be done about it.
I have been amazed at the growing practice in eastern Canada, the area east of the great lakes, of not eating much bread at meals. I have been at a loss to understand why, and have gone to considerable trouble to seek an explanation from the planners of meals, the wives and mothers. It appears to be the young wives and the young mothers who are the leaders in the curtailment of bread consumption. The one answer I get is that they really like bread but that it is not on their slimming diet.
Out on the prairies, Mr. Speaker, the young wives and mothers know the value of bread consumption, both for their health and for the welfare of the wheat producers who are either themselves or their neighbours. Many of them bake their own bread. One of the great pleasures of visiting in my constituency is to go into a home where there is the smell of home baked bread. I know of one young mother with four sons who must
The Budget-Mr. Pascoe bake a dozen loaves of bread each week. Her boys are the picture of health, and she is just as slim as those who avoid bread in their diets. What I am attempting to emphasize is that a larger consumption of bread would raise the domestic sales of flour milled from our good western wheat, and this would help to reduce our wheat surplus.
I have some figures for the United States which I think can be converted into comparable figures for flour consumption in Canada. Consumption of flour in the United States at the present time averages 119 pounds per year per capita, compared with an average of 160 pounds per capita in the period from 1935 to 1939. If Americans were consuming flour at the 1935 to 1939 rate it would mean using an additional 165 million bushels of wheat a year for milling purposes, or well over 1 billion bushels of wheat in the past 10 years. On the basis of the same estimate Canada, with a population about one tenth that of the United States, would have used an additional 100 million bushels of wheat in the form of flour in the last 10 years; and I think, Mr. Speaker, we would be a healthier people.
I have here a food chart issued by the health league of Canada. It is headed "Canada's Food Rules", and at the bottom is this notation:
Approved by the Canadian council on nutrition, nutrition division, Department of National Health and Welfare, Ottawa.
It is true that the chart was issued before the present government came into office, but in this connection I think the government in office at that time was on the right track. Foods are shown for a balanced diet, and the chart goes on to say:
These foods are good to eat. Eat them every day for health. Have at least three meals each day.
Under the heading "Cereals and bread" there is the following:
One serving of whole grain cereal and at least four slices of bread.
If each person in Canada, Mr. Speaker, ate four slices of bread a day the wheat marketing problem would be very much easier for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I should like to have that statement on the record as one way in which the Canadian people can help to reduce the wheat surplus.
Before I conclude I feel I must make reference to remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) about a divided Canada through what he referred to as "Quebec provincialism". The hon. member's remarks perhaps should not be taken too seriously, because he delights in making statements that receive headlines. In this particular case he probably was disappointed
3144	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Pearson because the headlines were not too many or too large. I am sorry he is not in the house to hear these remarks.
Quebec has shown little interest in his party at any time, and perhaps that is the reason for his statements. To me it is the old game of divide and conquer, or should I say attempt to divide and attempt to conquer. As I see it, the hon. member for Port Arthur realizes that the party of which I am a member is the one truly national party, the party of unity, the party of one Canada. His party thrives on disunity, on divided segments in our economy. His latest speech can be considered as an effort to drive a wedge between Quebec and the rest of Canada now that the two are coming closer together as a united Canada under the Progressive Conservatives.
Mr. Speaker, I do not need to speak for the Quebec members; they are well able to speak for themselves. As a member from a predominantly English speaking province I have been impressed with the way in which we have been able to work with our French speaking colleagues. I believe this holds out the best hope for Canadian unity; one Canada under this Progressive Conservative national government.
The hon. member for Port Arthur says Quebec members have little interest in national problems and are concerned only with Quebec matters. I do not agree with this view. I have found Quebec members very interested in our prairie problems and anxious to help us do something about them on a truly national level. I cannot speak too strongly against the regrettable statements of the hon. member for Port Arthur. He may speak for his group of eight members in this house, but I am sure he does not speak for the members of our party, nor does he speak in the interests of Canadian unity.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I may not have agreed with everything my hon. friend who has just taken his seat has said, but I certainly do agree with him in his last remarks. In this debate we are dealing primarily with the economic health of the nation, and we are talking about facts and figures which bear on that particular subject. However, in his last words the hon. member has made us aware of the fact there can be no prosperity, no stability, no economic progress or progress of any kind in this country unless we have national unity, something which I should like to think every member of this house, without exception, is interested in strengthening.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You are quite right in that assumption.
[Mr. Pascoe.l

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend will forgive me if I do not follow him in his very interesting discussion on how to eat wheat and grow slim and healthy. But like him I will be, in my contribution to this debate, using some facts and figures which have already been used and, like him, I make no apology for doing so because of the importance of the situation which these facts and figures portray.
On March 31, in his third budget the Minister of Finance, after previous budgetary deficits totalling more than a billion dollars and cash deficits totalling $2,300 million, announced that he was budgeting this year for a surplus of $12 million on an expenditure of $6,330 million. There remained, however, an estimated cash deficit for the current year of $210 million. This, Mr. Speaker, is in contrast to the experience of his predecessor who after three cash surpluses in a row and out of expenditures of $5,072 million had, in his last budget in 1957, a budgetary surplus of $258 million and a cash surplus of $424 million.
When we pointed out this contrast in the budget debate last year and expressed some anxiety about what these contrasting figures represented in terms of economic development in our country, we were accused by the minister and other members of the government and the government party of indulging in gloom. But the predictions made on this side in the budget debate last year as to what was likely to happen in the ensuing 12 months have been borne out by events. I remember saying, as recorded on page 2913 of last year's Hansard, in reference to the prediction made by my hon. friend:
I suggest his prediction of a 7 per cent increase-
He added, when he made the prediction, "with stable prices".
-may well be too optimistic, and that if the hon. gentleman is wrong in this calculation the effect on employment opportunities in 1959 and 1960 in this country will be very bad indeed.
What are the facts? Well, the gross national product increased in volume by 3.5 per cent.
In so far as employment is concerned I said, as recorded on page 2914 of Hansard for last year:
If only a 4 to 5 per cent increase in the volume of the gross national product is achieved ... that would mean that during the current year we would have, on the average, more than 300,000 people unemployed in this country which would be the second highest level in the post-war period.
What are the facts? The average number of unemployed during 1959 was 350,000, 50,000 more than the prediction I made which was considered to be too pessimistic.
In so far as inflation is concerned, I said I believed prices would rise in the current

year. The dominion bureau of statistics reports an increase of 2.3 per cent in final prices in 1959 as compared to a rise of 2.2 per cent in 1958. So, Mr. Speaker, predictions of that kind which were made last year, and which were criticized as being too pessimistic, have in some respects turned out to be not pessimistic enough in the light of events.
On March 31, 12 long days ago, we had from the minister the forecast of things to come in his budget speech this year. It was, of course, the minister's night, and I should like to congratulate him on his presentation. He made a fine appearance, and it was a fine presentation. There is, of course, as much difference-I know the minister will agree- between appearance and achievement as there is between a beauty queen parading in a bathing suit and swimming the English channel. Now the minister is in the swim, in the waters between Scylla and Charybdis, that is in the cold waters between Coyne and Churchill, pulled and pushed by opposing currents. On this occasion, however, on March 31, I think he was more Churchillian than he had been on previous occasions.
There have been some noticeable differences between the statements of the two ministers in the past few months on economic and financial matters, and on the nature and seriousness of our economic problems. There have been not only differences but there have been contradictions, and those contradictions on a few points have extended even to the facts. An example of this is to be found-this is only one example-by comparing a sentence from the minister's speech on March 31 and one from a speech made by his colleague on the same general subject on March 21. The minister is reported in Hansard, page 2672, as saying:
Since 1950 . .. the rate of increase in our net foreign indebtedness has exceeded the growth in national output.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce, as reported in Hansard, page 2281, on March 21, 1960 said that the rate of economic expansion had surpassed the rate of increase in Canadian foreign indebtedness. Well, which minister is right? You pay your taxes and you take your choice.
The difference between the minister, as he spoke on March 31, and the views of the governor of the Bank of Canada is somewhat more surprising because of the statement the minister had previously made, which seemed to harmonize with statements the governor of the Bank of Canada had been making. The governor of the bank said a few months ago in Winnipeg as follows, and I quote from his speech on that occasion:
The Budget-Mr. Pearson
Canadian savings and the machinery of the Canadian capital market can now supply all the capital funds needed by government and business combined to carry on a capital expenditure program as large in total as is sound and healthy for the Canadian economy to sustain in any one year.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce, of course, has not agreed with that statement, and has insisted in more than one statement that United States capital, in present circumstances, is necessary and desirable. The Minister of Finance himself on March 31 was not so much worried about this matter. He said, and I quote from Hansard at page 2674:
The economic expansion which Canada is now experiencing is soundly based.
He would go no further in caution on that occasion than this, and I quote from the same speech:
I do not anticipate that if we manage our affairs prudently and properly-
And what a government escape hatch that is.
-Canada will indefinitely continue to rely on capital from abroad as heavily as in the last few years.
That statement may be found at page 2672 of Hansard. There is quite a gap between the view of the governor of the Bank of Canada and the minister on that score. What a contrast between the attitude taken by the minister on this occasion and the Conservative election manifesto of 1957, which had this to say on this point:
In 1956 Canada achieved a frightening and perilous adverse balance of trade with the U.S of $12 billions.	'
I would call the attention of hon. members to that expression "balance of trade". That is an expression which, when I used it in a debate some time ago in this house, was contradicted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who said it was inaccurate and wrong. But on this Tory occasion it refers to trade both tangible and intangible. At that time in 1956 it was supposed to be frightening when the adverse balance of trade was $1.2 billion-"frightening and perilous" were the words used-but now when the figures are much higher they apparently no longer frighten hon. gentlemen opposite. The minister stated as follows:
We can look forward to another year of balanced growth.
That statement is to be found at page 2669 of Hansard. What a contrast that is not only to the election manifestos but to the minister's own speech of June 17, 1958, when our total deficits were much less than they are now but when he said, and I quote from

The Budget-Mr. Pearson a speech made in this house as reported at page 1237 of Hansard of that year:
-carry serious implications for the future health and economic independence of our country.
In the same speech the minister added:
The chronic nature of our massive trade imbalance with the U.S. requires ... energetic corrective measures.
That was at a time when the imbalance was not as serious as it is now. I ask whether this budget shows that we have or are getting these energetic corrective measures. That is our chief complaint or our major criticism against this budget. However, the minister tempered his optimism somewhat a week ago Thursday evening by this statement, which I quote from his speech. He said:
But, as my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, says: "We must not be complacent".
In singling out the Minister of Trade and Commerce as an exemplar of cautious realism, the minister has proved at least one thing, namely that he has a sense of humour, something about which there has apparently been some doubt in the past.
As I have already tried to point out in previous discussions of this matter, not only the amount but the nature of our unfavourable balance must cause anxiety. Last week in his budget speech the Minister of Finance said this:
What is important is that a substantial portion of these resources-
That is investments from abroad.
-should be put into new capital investment rather than into consumption and that this new investment should be of a character that will promote the efficiency and productivity of our country.
Then he added:
Broadly speaking I believe that this objective is being attained.
The facts show, Mr. Speaker, that it is not being attained nearly to the extent that it was being attained a few years back. Indeed, the facts show that the trend in the last year or two has been in the opposite direction.
Having delivered himself of some cheerful but, as we think, unrealistic predictions, the minister found that some of the figures he used in his own speech and some of the figures in the budget papers rather spoiled the effect of those predictions; because they showed-and I am going to mention only one or two of them-that in 1960-61 not only would Canadians pay nearly $600 million more in taxes than in 1959, but that in spite of these payments we would have a fourth consecutive cash deficit of about $210 'million.
As a consequence of this, the minister said he was not announcing but was looking forward to the day-and I quote from him-

-when we can undertake a measure of orderly reduction in our public debt.
That statement is to be found at page 2682 of Hansard. That was something we on this side of the house, when we were on the other side, could look backward to and not merely forward to. A budgetary surplus is, of course, a good thing, even a little one, provided it is achieved in the right way, through the right policies and of course not at the expense of even more important things than balancing the budget. In order to bring about his baby budgetary surplus the minister delayed action on any increases in civil service and armed forces salaries and then reduced such increases, when they were made, to a minimum. Further adjustments-and they undoubtedly will and should be made- will convert the present small budgetary surplus into a deficit. Indeed, other supplementary estimates may have that effect on the minister's already shakily balanced budget. How shakily it is balanced I shall hope to show by referring to some parts of the minister's statement itself and to the accompanying budgetary white paper.
The general situation, says the minister, is one of "balanced growth". But is it? The gross national product increased 3.5 per cent in volume in 1959. That is the first real increase since 1956, and of course it is welcome. But it is below the post-war average, and it is about one half what the minister himself estimated.
Mr. Pallet!: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is about one half the minister's own figure of what he estimated.
Mr. Pallet!: No; that is Martin figures you are using.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is the figure which is taken from the national accounts, income and expenditure. If my hon. friend who is sceptical about the matter will look at page 7, percentage changes in value, volume and price, he will see that the gross national expenditure volume in 1958 is up 3.5 per cent. Now, Mr. Speaker, a figure so far below the forecast for 1959-60 is surely not a very impressive basis for optimism based on predictions of a 6 per cent increase for 1960-61. If the minister is as far out this year as he was last year, the surplus will very quickly be converted into a deficit.
The minister gave us a good deal of advice in his speech. His policy to deal with any danger that might be ahead, particularly the danger of inflation on which he quite rightly spent some time and made some warning statements, is to advise us to work and save. That is good advice, but it is not as impressive as it might be coming from a government

which in about four years will have produced four cash deficits amounting to $2.5 billion and which, contrary to all its promises, has upped expenditures from $5,218 million in 1956-57 to $6,470 million in 1960-61.
This exhortation to work and save also comes from a government that has failed to do anything effective to prevent mass unemployment. We had the latest figures this afternoon which illustrate what we mean by mass unemployment at the end of March. The figure for unplaced applicants was 835,000, 53,400 more than at this time last year.
Mr. Speaker, those without work cannot save, as has already been pointed out in this debate. But the minister's treatment of this problem in his budget speech was pretty casual, and I will quote the passage in his speech dealing with it. He said, as reported at page 2670 of Hansard:
-as the result of an unusual Increase in the number of persons estimated to be in the labour force, the estimate of the numbers without jobs and seeking work was 18,000 higher than a year ago.
It is more than that now. The minister then went on:
I am confident, however, that employment will rise as the coming of spring opens up new job opportunities and as the economy continues its upward trend.
This might be called the meteorological approach to the problem of unemployment. It will go with the snow. I wish it were true, but the facts do not seem to bear out the prediction the minister has made. His assertion that the higher unemployment which he talked about was due to an unusual increase in the labour force is a misrepresentation of the facts. The increase in the labour force in I960 was not unusually high. The increase in the labour force in 1959 was unusually low, and if the minister will take a look at page 26 of his budget papers he will find statistics there to show this. Mr. Speaker, the fact is, as we have pointed out from this side of the house time after time, that seasonal unemployment is not only unusually high but has now become a chronic and serious problem about which something must be done.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What would the Liberal party do about it?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the Liberal party was in power there was never this kind of unemployment, but I will come to that later. We had our recessions in the period after 1945, and I will be very glad to show my hon. friend later in my speech how we dealt with the kind of recession and unemployment we had then, which was not nearly as high as it is now. Mr. Speaker, you would never
The Budget-Mr. Pearson realize this problem is as serious as it is from the minister's speech. "The coming of spring" is the only hopeful sign he can bring forward.
What about agriculture, about which the hon. member who preceded me had a good deal to say in his speech? I think I am right in saying that it is completely omitted from the minister's economic picture. The gross national product last year is up in value by 6 per cent. The net farm income, as has been pointed out more than once in this house, is down by 7 per cent. The estimated increase in the gross national product in the current year is another 6 per cent. The estimate for agriculture is another decline, I think of 7 per cent. That surely does not represent a balanced growth in a vital sector of our national economy. But there is not a word about this problem in the minister's statement.
Mr. Speaker, what about the Atlantic provinces? Is there balanced growth down there? We did not get a progress report from the minister in his budget statement on the realization of the Atlantic charter. And we know why. Since the 1958 election it would be difficult for the minister to point to anything that has been done for the Atlantic provinces except the establishment of royal commissions. It would be difficult for the minister to prove that economic conditions are not deteriorating in the Atlantic provinces at this time, especially in the coal industry, where I think the situation will be admitted by just observers to be about the worst in 50 years.
I know the minister was down in the Atlantic provinces not long ago. I was there a week after he was, in Halifax. The minister mentioned 21 things which had been done by this government for the Atlantic provinces, 18 of which had been initiated by the previous government. He included the construction of the Canso causeway. I am sure the 100 pipers who filed by Angus Macdonald on that great day were not participating in the realization of a Conservative vision.
That is perhaps one reason why the minister was silent about the situation in the Atlantic provinces. Of course he did say there would be a reduction of the sales tax on electrical heating equipment to permit-and I quote-"this method of household heating to compete for the market on the same terms as other methods of heating". That may be a very desirable thing to do, but it is no help to the coal industry in the Atlantic provinces except perhaps to help them tj live better electrically. Yet we are told that balanced

The Budget-Mr. Pearson growth has characterized the progress of the last year, and that our economic growth is soundly based.
Mr. Speaker, let me examine this policy in respect of the balance of payments situation and the premium on our dollar. I have already touched upon the minister's dilemma in this matter as illustrated by his own speeches, on some occasions as an economist and on other occasions as a politician. In these speeches, especially the one on budget night, he seems to me to be, as I have suggested, balanced uneasily between the warnings of Mr. Coyne and the hosannahs of Mr. Churchill, with one eye on the red light of the governor and the other on the green light of the minister. In a friendly way I would warn him that it will be difficult to maintain this ambiguous posture. It will require all the political and economic gymnastic ability of the Minister of Finance.
One aspect of this imbalance which has political as well as economic significance is the problem of foreign ownership and control, of course primarily by the United States. The passionate anxiety of the minister and his colleagues of other days has dwindled to the modest preoccupation with this particular subject shown in the budget speech. He indicated that no legislative or governmental action was required, that no special steps were necessary to encourage Canadian as opposed to foreign control. He suggested that we might leave it all to the Prime Minister's <Mr. Diefenbaker) great gift of persuasion, that gift of bedazzlement which at times deteriorates into a genius for befuddlement.
An Indian delegation visited the Prime Minister not so many weeks ago, and I think this was referred to by my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson). A member of the delegation is reported to have said with reference to the Prime Minister: "He is a great talker. He can almost make you forget what you came here for."
So the minister forgets his worries about swollen deficits and foreign control and assures us that our growing foreign-held debt can easily be borne. He does that, as some of his colleagues have also done, by making what can only be described as a phony relationship between the foreign-held debt and our gross national product, as if the latter-the gross national product-represented any adequate measure of our ability to pay our debt in foreign currency.
The minister is not too worried. I quote again from his speech at page 2674 of Hansard:
So long as our access to foreign markets is unimpaired and we are able to keep the cost and the
(Mr. Pearson.]

quality of our products and services thoroughly competitive, we need have no fears for the future.
But there are others who are more worried than the minister and they are not all members of the Liberal opposition. Indeed, they included the minister himself on earlier occasions and they certainly include the governor of the Bank of Canada. There are people in this country who are worried about our increasing total trade imbalance, our increasing foreign-held debt and the high external price of our dollar which is a special problem especially in connection with export trade which must increase if we are to go ahead.
The minister expressed the other night the thought that the premium on our dollar could be reduced without the necessity of any form of governmental action even though I suggested governmental action-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the hon. gentleman saying that I said that?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes. I am saying that the minister said he hoped this situation could correct itself without any form of governmental control.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, that is different.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But the minister did not suggest any governmental action that might be taken to correct it, either.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We took it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister made no suggestion for any kind of governmental action to correct the situation. He did say it should not be done by any form of governmental control but I suggest to the minister that governmental action is largely responsible for this particular situation and I will try to explain how.
Our money supply, as the minister knows, has been stable since October, 1958. Out of this constant supply the government borrowed in 1959, $871 million or 52 per cent of all the bonds marketed in that year. That governmental demand, of course, was a major factor in creating a scarcity of funds for others, in pushing interest rates up so high and in bringing about tight money. The result of that was that the provinces and municipalities had to borrow their money in the United States market. In 1959 the net amount so borrowed was $400 million which is a record. It represents 27 per cent of our net import of foreign capital that year. That itself is a major cause of our dollar premium and for that the federal government must accept much of the responsibility.
What about the situation in the current year in regard to borrowing? Of course, it should be much easier for the provinces

and municipalities. They have no desire to go to the United States money market to satisfy their financial needs. If they can get their money in Canada at reasonable rates it is not necessary to urge or compel them to do that. All that is required is to leave them some room in the Canadian market, to stop hogging it and to stop pushing interest rates up. I suggest that that would be a very simple way of reducing the premium on our dollar without recourse to controls which, I quite agree with the minister, should be put into effect only in an emergency and as a last resort; that is, a complete system of government exchange control.
I certainly do not advocate that in the present circumstances. The borrowing requirements for 1960-61 represent for the federal government-they come from a cash deficit-about $210 million but of course they may be more. Even if they do not increase they represent a substantial but I agree it is well below last year's figure which was approximately $900 million. That should be all to the good in regard to financing in Canada but I should like to call the minister's attention-and perhaps it is not needed-to a new factor which is arising and which will hinder this development and which is in its turn, if I may use the expression, a hangover from that conversion loan about which the minister and the government still boast.
To ensure the success of that loan the Bank of Canada had to buy very substantial amounts of the outstanding bonds which it converted into long term conversion bonds. In fact, by the end of October, 1958 the Bank of Canada held more than $1,200 million of all bonds with maturities of 10 years or more compared with $300 million before the conversion loan was undertaken. The bank naturally found itself subsequently in a very illiquid, inflexible position. Its holdings were mainly of bonds not maturing for several years.
The Bank of Canada is apparently at the present time attempting to correct the situation by selling long term conversion bonds to the public and with the proceeds buying treasury bills and other short term securities. That is driving down the treasury bill and the bank rates, already weakening under lessening demand, and is keeping the long term interest rates higher than they otherwise would be. It also means that the bank is now doing what the government did last year, competing with the provinces and municipalities for long term money in Canada.
This policy of the bank if it is continued, along with the necessity for the government to meet its own cash requirements, may well mean that the provinces and municipalities 79951-0-199
The Budget-Mr. Pearson will not find it much easier in 1960 than in 1959 to satisfy their borrowing requirements in Canada and they may be forced once again to go to the United States market thereby keeping up an artificially high premium on our dollar.
Therefore, instead of trotting out the bugbear of controls the minister should have faced up to this problem realistically and responsibly because the government is largely responsible for it. It is one of the problems that should temper the excessive optimism about the situation in the current year.
On what does the minister base this optimism? As I have said, for the coming year the minister forecasts a gross national product increase of 6 per cent. He leaves out the condition that this will occur if it is a year with stable prices. If that 6 per cent is meant to be an increase in volume it will probably turn out to be optimistic. If it is a 6 per cent increase in value, and if the price level moves about the same this year as it did last year, it would means about a 3.5 per cent increase in volume. I would think that might be a reasonable forecast. But, if it turned out to be a reasonable forecast it would mean that for the fourth consecutive year the gross national product increase would be below the post-war average. Is that a reason, then, for booming optimism?
For the year as a whole all the main components are expected to rise: new investment, 4 per cent; total business investment, excluding agriculture and fisheries, about 7 per cent, although in the United States it is 14 per cent; but in constant dollars it will be lower than in 1957, and yet the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) says: "Business confidence is high" and all is well.
One thing is sure, Mr. Speaker. Even on the basis of the minister's own forecast these trends, prospects and estimates are not sufficient ground for hoping for any material improvement on the unemployment front. In 1959 employment rose 2.7 per cent but unemployment was higher than in any postwar year except 1958, and almost equalled that. That situation would have been worse but for the lowest increase in the labour force experienced in recent years, not an unusually high increase, but the lowest increase in the labour force experienced in recent years, an increase of 1.6 per cent as against an average of 4 per cent in 1957. The minister can get these figures from his own budget papers at page 27.
With a normal increase in the labour force this year the average level of unemployment in the current year might well exceed that of 1959, and surely that is a cause for worry and no ground for complacency of any kind.

The Budget-Mr. Pearson The minister may say, "Well, the gross national product increase will take care of it". Even on the basis of the minister's own estimates, this well may happen; especially in view of the minister's statement, and I quote from page 2674 of Hansard:
The rate of Increase we have experienced in 1959 should be maintained throughout the year.
I suggest that prophecy is of doubtful validity. I should like to explain why I suggest the minister may be too optimistic in his view of the prospects.
The so-called short business cycle, mainly caused by fluctuations, I suppose, in inventories, has always been quite a regular feature of our economy. If we accept the years immediately after world war II, we are now going through the third of those cycles in the post-war period. During this post-war period we experienced recessions in 1948-49, 195354 and 1957-58, each one worse than the one preceding it. We are told by experts- and I think the facts bear it out-that we have been on the upturn since April, 1958. Past experience and certain trends indicate that a fourth post-war cycle may develop again soon. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we should be prepared for it; surely, we should plan against the danger of its recurrence before long.
Economic forecasters themselves agree that we shall have a recession soon, but most of them differ as to its timing. I am quoting now from economists who have certainly no political axe to grind in this matter. The most optimistic outlook for the future was presented by the economic advisers of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Dr. Firestone, in a speech on October 24, 1959, said this, and I quote one paragraph from his speech:
Looking ahead to the immediate future, we can see a fair rate of increase in economic activity for 1960 and possibly 1961... If anything, the problems that we may be encountering as we go into 1962 may be more difficult to deal with than those we encountered in the post-war period. What I am implying is that the recession we may be facing in 1962 could be more extensive than anything we have yet experienced since the end of world war II, and it may require quite vigorous action to reduce its extent in terms of length of time and the severity of the economic downturn.
That is Dr. Firestone in a speech last October, but since October other expert economic analysts have produced more and more evidence that another recession may begin sooner than expected by Dr. Firestone. In its tax memo on the federal budget outlook published in February, 1960, a document with which 1 am sure the minister is quite familiar, the Canadian Tax Foundation refers to the possibility of a downturn in the current fiscal year. The same warning is given in the last three

business forecasts issued by General Research Associates from Toronto. Here is what these experts had to say in January about general economic conditions that we may expect in 1960, and I quote from their forecast. They say:
The chances are better than ever that the next business cycle peak will occur in the fourth quarter of 1960 or the first quarter of 1961. The more rapid the intervening buildup-and the more closely it is related to inventory building-the greater is the probability of the earlier downturn.
That was their January bulletin. They followed that up with their March bulletin, when they were a little more precise. They had this to say:
In general summary, there has been little evidence to suggest that the current prosperity will last much beyond the third quarter of 1960. Such evidence as has appeared in the last two or three months would suggest, if anything, an earlier downtrend.
That is from their March bulletin. Their latest forecast for April, which has just come out, had this to say:
The contrast produced by the shades of light and dark is typical of the turbulence that occurs just prior to the end of a business upswing.
These expert and objective forecasts do not support the rosy picture which is painted by the minister and the government. Perhaps the trade and commerce "hidden report" would be equally cautious if we were allowed to see it. Perhaps it may have warnings which explain why it has been secreted, although the issues of 1957 and 1958 were made public in dramatic circumstances.
I ask the Minister of Finance, does the government recognize any of those omens, or does it merely intend to bury its head in the sands of self-satisfaction? Does it not realize that the financial position is such that the government will be seriously handicapped in facing any new recession which, according to Dr. Firestone, may be more extensive than any we have experienced since the end of world war II? These problems are not imaginary. To apreciate them we have only to look at the year 1960, not in isolation but in relation to the recent past.
Compare the business cycle through which we are going with the one before, both in regard to changes in the gross national product and in the financial position of the government. For the purpose of making the comparison I should like, if the house agrees, to insert in Hansard at this point two tables taken from official statistics, one giving the actual changes in the volume of the gross national product since 1953, expressed as a percentage of the previous year. The other table is the budgetary and cash position of the Canadian government since the fiscal year ended March, 1954.

speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Pearson unsettled fiscal relations with the provinces and growing dependence in defence and development on the United States of America?
The minister's budget speech and the budget itself ignored these problems. So I ask the minister to tell us, if a recession should recur-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Wouldn't the Liberals be glad.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-with the government's financial position weaker than at the beginning of the last one-that, of course, was quite an unworthy comment by my hon. friend. When we point out these possibilities which are also being pointed out by men who are not interested in politics at all hon. gentlemen not only accuse us of gloom and doom but of playing politics in doing our duty and indicating what may happen. So I ask the minister, and I make no apology for asking him, if a recession should recur, with the government's financial position weaker than it was at the beginning of the last one and with a continuing high level of unemployment, what are the government's plans and its policies to meet that contingency in a way which will recognize its responsibilities to maintain full employment and financial stability?
Will the government once again fall back on a series of huge, unplanned deficits which add new rigidities to our economic and fiscal structure, higher interest rates, without creating anything like full employment? That has been our experience in the last few years. Will the government once again rely on solemn sermons and emotional appeals, while getting the Bank of Canada to bail it out through another round of rapid credit expansion and monetary inflation?
If the minister cannot answer these questions, what right has he to claim, as he did in his budget speech, that he is "fully aware of the role of leadership that falls to the federal government"? If the government is really aware of its role of leadership, why are we not getting it instead of expedients designed to paper over the cracks or, to cite an analogy a little more topical in Ottawa at this time, to fill up the potholes? Surely there is no leadership in waiting for something to turn up, which this budget does; or the philosophy that we will jump off that bridge when we come to it. I quote from an editorial in the Hamilton Spectator of April 6, a newspaper that is not notoriously friendly to the Liberal party:
Mr. Fleming may be accused of lacking leadership. In a sense he has stepped to the sidelines and left us to look after our salvation with a mild word of advice.


There is no leadership in merely telling Canadians to manage their own affairs better, to show self-restraint and caution, to work and save. As the Globe and Mail, another newspaper not notoriously friendly to this party, put it on April 4:
We wish Mr. Fleming would manage his own affairs as prudently as he exhorts the Canadian people to manage theirs.
In default of plans and policies of their own to deal with these matters the government look at us and implore, what would you do? In the first place we would have put into effect three years ago fiscal policies which would have prevented many of the difficulties in which we find ourselves now, those Liberal fiscal and financial policies which met previous recessions successfully. They have been put forward more than once and proof of their effectiveness is found in the history of Canada from 1940 to 1957. One reason we are now facing the difficult problems which we are facing in this field today is that this kind of financial policy was not followed.
I have tried to state what the difficulties are, even if the minister has not. To face them frankly, to be aware of them, is the first and indispensable step in their solution. Hon. members are continually saying, what would you do? On several occasions in this session we have said what we would do about unemployment; we have said what we would do about agricultural conditions, support prices for eggs, hogs instead of deficiency payments; we have said what we would do in trying to stimulate our export trade. When we have made these proposals we have raised them in concrete form. What does the government do? It ignores them completely. When we try to raise these problems in the field of defence, where we are spending $1,500 million which would be a great help in meeting some of these financial problems, what does the government do? It refuses to even give us the right to discuss these problems effectively. Then they continue to say, what would you do? When we tell them what we would do, they ignore our suggestions or refuse us the right to even discuss them.
There is one more point I want to emphasize before I conclude. In defence, and in every other form of governmental activity, every single dollar of unnecessary expense must be eliminated. This, however, does not mean, as we see it on this side, that for desirable social purposes, such as the restoration and development of depressed areas, the government should hesitate to spend the money which is required where private enterprise cannot do the job alone or at all.

Furthermore, in a general economic emergency, not the kind of recession we have had since world war II, but in a general economic emergency which I hope we will not have, the kind of emergency we had in the 30's, with massive unemployment even worse than we have today, no government should be afraid of a deficit, provided that deficit is planned and designed to achieve the social and economic purposes in mind and is not one accumulated through the implementation of un-co-ordinated political commitments, as were the deficits of my hon. friend in the last two years. There should also be the proviso that it be made clear, in any proposal that is made, that all expenditures can only come, either immediately or ultimately, from the pockets of the taxpayers. There is no other way. It is important to balance our national budget. It may be important, in certain circumstances to budget for a surplus. But there is an objective of government more important even than these, to keep free people working and a stable country expanding. Good social purposes should not be subordinated even to fiscal policies. The two must go hand in hand, each one supporting the other. This requires wisdom, imagination and courage on the part of governments at all levels. It requires hard work and common sense on the part of the citizens. This is a combination, Mr. Speaker, that should underlie Canada's development in the years ahead and can ensure, in so far as national policy can ensure, a good future for our country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome more than I can adequately say the opportunity of following immediately after the speech by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) this afternoon. Before I address myself to replying to some of his observations, may I turn back to these seven days that the budget debate has progressed and express to many hon. members who have spoken in the course of this debate my very deep sense of gratitude for the most kind things that they have said about the budget and the effort that was devoted to it. These things mean a great deal to me, and I do wish to convey my sense of appreciation of them.
The debate has, by this time, come to be impressed with several features. In this respect I think probably we have had less contributed to the features of this debate by the opposition than is usual in this annual debate. It is evident, I think, that the dominant note throughout this debate has been a positive and constructive note struck by those hon. members supporting the government who have seen fit to speak of the
The Budget*-Hon. D.M. Fleming budget and the fundamental objects in the Canadian economy which this budget is designed to serve. But if there has been a contribution to this debate by hon. members of the official opposition I say, Mr. Speaker, that it has been distinguished by two features. The first is that the opposition has no alternative and no policy to offer to the Canadian people. The second is that they are lost in gloom of their own creation.
Let me enlarge on these two points. We have been waiting patiently during these seven days of debate for some indication, at least some outline, of what hon. members opposite say ought to be done in these circumstances by a budget that this budget does not do, or what a budget ought not to do that this budget has done. We have waited, even to the last minute of the speech by the Leader of the Opposition, for some statement of the policy of the Liberal party and what they say they would do under those circumstances were they transferred to this side of the house. We have been waiting, and we have not heard.
A glorious opportunity was given to the financial critic of the opposition, not only when he spoke to the house a week ago yesterday, and it was a great opportunity that was given then, but also on a certain television program in which that distinguished hon. gentleman participated during the same week. If I may attempt to summarize the course of the press interview on the television program, it came down to this: Time and again those who participated in the questioning urged, asked, begged, the hon. gentleman to answer this question, what would you do under these circumtances? Two things emerged crystal clear from the replies of that hon. gentleman. Oh, how constructive were those replies, Mr- Speaker. He said in the first place,-and I tell you this is a constructive answer-"We would consult the experts".

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It might have been a good idea if you had done so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is rather hard on Professor Lamontagne. The financial critic certainly down-graded the Liberal professorial brain trust. But he did not stop there. Oh, no; he had a second answer, firm, courageous and constructive. This is what he said. When pressed again with this question "What would you do?" his answer was, "We would do something". That is the content of the whole press interview as to what he would have done or what his party would have done under these circumstances.
We have now heard the Leader of the Opposition. He has had the benefit of another

The Budget-Hon. D.M. Fleming week to think over this problem. He has had the opportunity of many more days in which to consult such experts as he sees fit to consult. He has had the benefit of some well-meant admonitions from many of the organs of the Liberal press in this country. What does he come up with?
It was in his final paragraph that he reached the great peroration in his remarks this afternoon. Oh, how thrilled we were. He was going to answer this question. We waited. We moved to the edge of our seats. We pricked up our ears. We became tense. Excitement rose, I am sure, in every bosom. Our hearts began to beat faster. At last we were going to be let in on the great Liberal secret and be told what they would do in these circumstances. Then out came the answer. How profound it was and right to the point. How forthright it was. There was no beating about the bush. Here is what he said. He said, "We would have put into effect Liberal fiscal policies three years ago".
Then he was asked from various parts of the house what those policies were. He did not have an answer and we are still waiting to hear it. We know just as much about what those policies are as we did before the hon. gentleman came to the beginning of his peroration or indeed before he began to speak this afternoon. He is still going on talking. It is the same old Liberal tactic. He talks about Liberal fiscal policies but he does not come down to earth and tell anybody what they are.
Then when he was pressed again by hon. gentlemen on this side of the house who said, "Tell us what are these policies", the best that anybody could get out of him was this; and I remind the house that he had unlimited time in which to speak today. He was not the least bit hurried. He had ample time in which to answer that question. He said, "We have said what we would have done". Does anybody remember his having said anything that they would have done under these circumstances? One can only conclude-and I am sure that this is a conclusion that only those among us most charitably disposed toward the Leader of the Opposition would reach under these circumstances-that what he is saying is that the policies they would have put into effect are those Liberal fiscal policies which led this country into the recession of 1957-58 and which the people of this country rejected in 1957 and again in 1958 at the polls in the most decisive manner.
I said there was a second feature contributed to this debate by the Liberal participants in it. It was indeed the contribution of gloom. To those who believe in the two-party system I must say in deep earnestness

that it fills some of us with deep concern to see the Liberal party wallowing in gloom concerning Canada. Perhaps it is not unnatural for them, on looking at their particular situation, to be afflicted with feelings of despondency. But why do they have to go further and try to transfer that gloom to Canada? In any event, I believe their efforts are not being crowned with success. Indeed, they are being crowned, on the part of the Canadian people, with the displeasure and disapproval which those tactics on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite so abundantly deserve. All their chagrin and all their disappointment at the failure of their gloomy predictions will be no justification in the minds of the Canadian people for their efforts to pour gloom and pessimism over the Canadian scene.
Indeed, hon. gentlemen opposite have not been satisfied with the facts. The facts are not in accord with the kind of conclusion they want people to draw and so they must put a gloss on the facts. We have witnessed some extraordinary things in this debate. It evidently matters not in their calculations whether what they say does harm to Canada as long as it serves the partisan interests of the Liberal party. I suppose this procedure makes no great impression in this house. We have heard them previously. We have seen them indulging in these tactics which have become chronic on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite since they went into opposition. I suppose there are not too many Canadians who do not see through this political game. But I believe that these statements do Canada's name harm outside of Canada.
I had occasion last summer when in London to be confronted with a number of articles concerning Canada in some of the economic journals in the United Kingdom. They were dismal in their reading of the trends of the Canadian economy. Where did those impressions arise? They certainly did not arise from the facts for at that very time Canadians were earning more than ever before, saving more than ever before, spending more than ever before and more were employed than ever before. One could point to a host of other facts. These facts had not registered there but the gloom had made some impression. If that had any relationship with facts in this country I can trace it to one source and one source only and that is to the kind of statements that have come from the Leader of the Opposition and his followers.
But the matter did not stop there. It has just gone on in the same way. In recent days they have endeavoured to quote back

to us-and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) did so a week ago yesterday-some of the articles in newspapers in the United Kingdom based not on the facts but on the kind of statements that have emanated from hon. members opposite. I think the situation has reached the point where hon. members opposite owe it to themselves as well as to the country and to the two-party system to examine themselves and to examine the tone and the trend of their remarks. I tell you that this kind of gloom in which they are indulging is not the kind of thing that is going to enable the Liberal part to fulfil its function and the future it thought it had in the two-party system.
I am speaking in this debate, Mr. Speaker, as one who is a firm believer in the two-party system and does not wish to see the Liberal party dig its own grave in dismal gloom. This has reached the stage of irresponsibility. Remember it is not so very long ago, just a year ago in the budget debate, when the Leader of the Opposition, as reported on page 2912 of Hansard for April 21, 1959, was saying:
X tell him-
That is the Minister of Finance.
-and the government that the word of Canada does not mean as much now as it did.
He was not satisfied to say that things were not going right; he was impugning the honour of this country in saying that Canada's word was not as good as it used to be. There seems to be-

If there is any doubt about it, then I say at once that I adopt the sentiments expressed in this very interesting piece of writing as my own. The heading is: "Liberals Keep 'Em Yawning", and it states:
The Liberal party had better get some policies or else stop holding press conferences.
This conclusion was forced on us by watching three parliamentary correspondents diligently but vainly trying to extract some clear answers from William Benidickson, Liberal financial critic on the C.B.C.'s televised "Press Conference" Tuesday night.
In the Commons, Mr. Benidickson had called Hon. Donald Fleming's budget a "do-nothing"

budget. Then what, asked the correspondents, would Mr. Benidickson have done in Mr. Fleming's place?
If he knew, Mr. Benidickson wasn't telling. He was true to the Liberal high command's policy of no-policy, of criticizing the government's action without offering alternatives. This is producing some of the most barren press conferences on record.
Would the Liberals raise taxes? No. Would they cut taxes? Well... perhaps some taxes on production.
Mr. Benidickson replied to some topical questions by recalling bold, wise moves the Liberals had taken in comparable circumstances when they were in power. For example, their emergency import restrictions to conserve American dollars in 1947.
We have news for Mr. Benidickson and the Liberal strategists: The voters don't care a hoot what the Liberals did in 1947. They just might be interested in Liberal remedies for the country's ills in 1960.
Mr. Benidickson viewed unemployment with justifiable concern. But he didn't say what the Fleming budget should have done about it.
Like other Liberal spokesmen, Mr. Benidickson offered two excuses for his unresponsiveness:
(1) The duty of the opposition is to criticize, not originate policies: (2) The opposition, being out of power, lacks access to the facts on which to base policies.
These excuses won't wash. It's true that the main job of the opposition, in parliament, is to expose government errors and omissions. But when a politician calls a press conference, or accepts an invitation to one, people expect some information, some constructive opinions. Fence-sitting and roundabout evasions make dull copy and dull T.V.
As for the excuse of lacking access to the facts, this might justify-but only in part-the Liberals' uncertainty on defence policy. The government does reserve important information in this field. In the others, plenty is known.
Unless the Liberals have some ideas and the courage to state them, they had better stay off television, for the sake of the party, as well as the viewers.
