I do not want to reflect in any way upon the decision of the committee; it is certainly an overwhelming majority which desires not to concern itself with the children and the effects on them. I am not reflecting on the wishes of the committee; I expressed my own feeling by voting as I did, and in my remarks prior to making the motion.
I come now to the petition. I think it is proper for us to make reference to particular items in order to see whether certain things have been proved.
The petition says in paragraph 1:
That on the 24th day of January, 1957, your petitioner-was lawfully married to the said-in the city of Pointe Claire, district of Montreal, in the province of Quebec.
There is evidence in paragraph No. 4 that the petitioner and the respondent lived and cohabited together. In paragraph No. 5 it is indicated that two children were born of the marriage. To the extent that it is necessary to prove, or to indicate that the marriage was consummated, this is one way in which consummation is proved. Since children were born of the particular marriage, to that extent we are duly bound to take cognizance of the particular material shown in the petition itself, and also of the corroborating evidence given later on.
Paragraph No. 6 of the petition makes reference to a certain matter which by itself does not seem to be in keeping with the orders of the other place relating to divorce, but I expect this is cleared up and permits us to overlook the fact that it does not comply with the standing orders of the other place. Paragraph No. 6 states:
That in the month of June 1958, your petitioner became suspicious that the said-had previously on divers occasions committed adultery with divers women whose names are unknown to your petitioner.
It is this reference which I submit is not in keeping with the rules of the other place relating to this matter. However, paragraph No. 7 is more specific, and makes reference to adultery having taken place on a particular day with a particular person and at a particular address. I would imagine that this is the reason why the members in the other place overlooked the conflict between this paragraph and the previous paragraph which refers to adultery in a sort of general way. Without discussing it, I am assuming this is the reason they overlooked the conflict with their standing orders.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
In order to prove this particular point, certain questions are asked by the clerk of the committee of the petitioner. The first proof required is that of the marriage having taken place. The petitioner was sworn and the clerk of the committee asked these questions:
Q. Are you married and, if so, to whom?
A. Yes, I am married to-.
Q. When were you married?
A. January 24, 1957.
Q. Do you remember by whom?
The name of the clergyman and the name of the church were given. I continue:
Q. I show you a document. Do you recognize this?
A. Yes, it is my marriage certificate.
Q. Are the names and dates correct?
A. Yes.
There is reference in the petition to the fact that two children were born, and the petitioner gives evidence to this effect, as was indicated by the hon. member for Halifax, and by the questions asked of the petitioner by Mr. Leggat, Q.C., counsel for the petitioner. He makes reference to the children having been born. For instance, on page 9 he asks this question:
Q. Did you have the baby?
A. Yes, I had the baby in August of 1957.
At various places throughout the evidence questions are asked as to the children, their ages, and other facts regarding them, to indicate that consummation of the marriage had taken place.
There is also a great deal of reference, as was indicated by the hon. member for Halifax, to how the children were to be looked after, what was the financial position of the petitioner and whether she would be able to care properly and adequately for them. There was reference to her being an ophthalmologist and to the fact that she was living with her mother. She is not working on a full-time basis. She has worked in a number of cities in eastern Canada. The amount of her income was referred to. There was also reference to the fact that her mother is caring for the children while she is away. A baby sitter does come in and does work but the mother is there most of the time.
There is also reference to the fact of the mother raising two small children, which indicates she is not sure whether she will have any difficulty in raising them. On page 12 she says:
As long as I am able to continue this work.
Senator Taylor questioned her about her present income, and she indicated that if she were sick or had to stop work it might be awkward but she is sure some arrangement could be made. There is extended reference to the children.

I submit that to some extent we should consider the fact that there are children is proof that the marriage has been consummated. We should consider the children to that extent, although we are forbidden by the rules and by a vote of this committee to concern ourselves any further with their welfare.
In this particular case, as the hon. member for Halifax indicated very succinctly and clearly, an extremely strange relationship existed prior to the actual case coming before us with respect to adultery having been proved. There is a great deal of reference about the physical and mental condition of the husband. I think we should concern ourselves with the aspect of mental cruelty which might lead up to adultery having taken place.
The evidence indicates that they lived at a particular address; that she was a student at McGill and he was working at Canadair. I am reading from page 9 of the evidence. The evidence says:
But he soon left Canadair and he wasn't working at all, he was sitting around writing.
Q. Writing what?
A. Poems.
Q. What happened during the months of February and March, 1957?
A. Well, I wasn't allowed to see anybody or talk to anybody. He was always arguing with me and swearing at me and calling me names and beating me up and he wouldn't let me out of the house and he wouldn't let my mother see me or come to see me.
Q. Did he virtually keep you a prisoner in the home?
A. It was pretty well like that. I suppose 1 could have skipped lectures but I was a student and he knew what my timetable was and if I didn't come right in on the dot he would beat me up or something. Then I was pretty worried too because I was pregnant and I was afraid that I would lose the child or something like that.
Then there is a question by Senator Isnor and the answer is a reiteration of the date when this occurred. Then Mr. Leggat continued:
Q. Did he ever actually cause you any bodily harm?
A. Yes, he did. He hurt me very badly and he made my ear bleed once, I remember. I was always covered with bruises. So I went to Mr. Leggat to see if I could do anything about it, and he said we could try to get a separation.
Then there is some reference to a separation. There is also indication of the respondent's lack of concern for the welfare of his wife and the two young children. There is evidence that would lead one to believe that he has a completely irresponsible attitude which in my submission is a form of mental cruelty. The respondent left at one stage and she did not hear from him for some time. When she did hear from him after the first 79951-0-200J
Private Bills-Divorce child was born he was in British Columbia. She had this to say as found on page 9 of the evidence:
A. I saw him once or twice in the spring of that year-
I would think that would be 1957.
-and then he left in June and then I heard from him again at the end of August after the baby was born, from British Columbia, and he had a job lined up there for teaching the following year and be asked me to go out and bring the baby and live in Prince George, British Columbia, but he didn't offer to pay for me to get out there or to pay the doctor's bills for the baby or for the hospital when the baby was born, or anything for my keep in all that time.
Q. And did you go out and try to make a go of it in British Columbia?
A. Yes, I did. I went out at the end of September, 1957. I had hoped if he was working again things would be different-
Then she indicates that he did pay some expenses for the upkeep of the house and herself there. She goes on to say:
He had been there about two months before I arrived and he had his group of friends and everything and he had various women who would drop around to the house quite frequently, and whenever they were there he seemed to ignore me and he would get very irritated if the baby cried and interrupted his conversation. Again it was the same thing, arguing with me and beating me.
So there is a repetition of what had happened before so far as cruelty is concerned and lack of concern for the wife and the child. In one instance he left in 1957 and she did not hear from him for some time. Then she did hear from him and she went out with the baby to Prince George, British Columbia. Then she was asked this question:
Q. What happened in the spring of 1958?
A. Eventually he suddenly told me one day he had given notice to the landlord and I would have to leave, and he wasn't going to keep on this house that we had and I might as well go back home, that he didn't want me. I suggested finding some other place and he really blew up then and he said no, that I could go back to my family in Montreal.
Q. He sent you back?
A. Yes, he pretty well did.
By Senator Barbour:
Q. Did he pay your way back?
A. No, he didn't. I borrowed money for that.
Q. He really abandoned you out there in the west?
A. It was pretty well that. I didn't know anyone there. There was no one I could stay with and he made no alternative arrangement. He just sort of dropped me.
Following that the young lady returned to her mother in Montreal in April, 1958. She is asked a question about the next time she saw the respondent, her husband and she gave this answer:
A. He came back to Montreal in June of 1958 and he phoned me up one day to say he was in Montreal but he didn't say what he was doing or anything, and he was not working. I had another baby coming in November but he didn't show any interest particularly in that or in the child we

Private Bills-Divorce already had, and he would call me up from time to time. He came to see me once and to see the little boy and he didn't offer to support me or anything or to pay any of the medical expenses and he Wouldn't tell me what he was doing or anything, and I asked him and he said he was just sitting around in his room doing nothing.
So we can assume that as far as the attitude of the husband is concerned it is a case of desertion. We are not duty bound to grant divorces on the basis of adultery and neither is the other place so even though there appears to be an unconscious desire to insist that some evidence of adultery be presented I submit that desertion would be the ground for the granting of a divorce in this case. I think the members of the committee of the other place gave the greatest weight to the questions of cruelty and desertion. I have only made reference to the evidence in that regard to show how extensive it was and how much the members of the other place were concerned with cruelty and desertion and with the lack of consideration by the husband for the welfare of the wife and the children.
I submit that this evidence influenced the members of the other place to a much greater extent than did the evidence of adultery and I think it is evidence which would properly influence us in granting this petition for divorce and dissolution of the marriage. But inasmuch as there is a desire to prove that adultery did in fact take place there is evidence given to this effect. I should like to make one or two comments about the evidence and the manner in which it was obtained. Evidence was given by Mr. George Roland Faucher who is an investigator and appeared as a witness on behalf of the petitioner. He was questioned extensively by Mr. Leggat and by the senators as found on pages 13, 14, 15 and 16. I might add that while there were two investigators involved in this case one of them died subsequent to the investigation and before the evidence was submitted to the committee so that only one individual gave evidence on behalf of the petitioner. He indicates that on a particular day they appeared at a certain address and noticed certain things. He was questioned by Mr. Leggat, as found on page 14:
Q. Do you know the apartment number?
The reference is to the particular address where adultery was supposed to have taken place or where it was indicated that it could have taken place.
A. Apartment 4 on the first floor, just to the right of the staircase.
Q. What did you do after you met him at 9 o'clock?
A. We waited until about 10.45 and decided we would try to go in and if he answered the door and was fully dressed we would use an excuse and walk away. We made our way to the first


floor and I knocked at the door which was opened a few moments later by Mr. Ramshaw, who was wearing a dark brown dressing gown and a pair of soft shoes. As the door opened toward the left we were able to see to the right that the woman was in the room-
Here again is evidence, I think, of illegal entry on the part of some of these investigators in their attempt to get evidence in order to prove certain circumstances which might lead us to reasonably assume that adultery could have or may have taken place. He said:
-and I pushed in and was followed by Mr. Maisonneuve-
This is the other investigator.
-I asked him to close the door behind me. As he opened the door I asked him if he was Mr.-, and he said yes, and I seen the woman and we both rushed in and I asked Mr. Maisonneuve to close the door.
There is an indication of illegal entry or trespass, pushing their way into someone else's private sanctum. I submit this is an invasion of the rights of the individual which should not be countenanced. I believe it is a criminal act, contrary to the Criminal Code, and that charges could be pressed for trespass or illegal entry. At least, as I have had this section of the Criminal Code explained to me I have been led to believe this could be done when evidence of this nature is given. These men both rushed in. You do not use the word "rush" or "push" if there is an invitation from an individual to enter. I continue to quote:
I then produced this photograph and asked him if it was one of himself, and he looked at it and said yes. He wanted to know what it was all about and I proceeded to tell him but he was angry-
I would assume that under normal circumstances he would be angry if two strangers were to push their way in or rush in and close the door. Up until this time, if this was not an arranged case, the respondent did not know that these particular investigators were coming to visit him at this particular time. He could come to the conclusion that all sorts of things might be the case. It might be an attempted robbery. I do not know what thoughts would go through his mind, but certainly there was reason for him to be angry.
-he was angry by the fact we were both in the room, and the woman was to our right in the bed and, as far as questioning our legality, we have a warrant-
I do not know whether or not, legally, they would be entitled to obtain a warrant for this particular type of activity. I would assume that warrants are granted to official police constables from time to time by the courts. I could not say whether or not these

gentlemen would have a warrant, but I would doubt it very much. In any event, the evidence goes on:
*-and as I tried to calm him down and explain the purpose of the call he became angry, and I finally threatened him that if he didn't quieten down and listen to me I would call the neighbours and Mrs.-, who I think was the home operator.
So we have here, one, invasion of rights contrary to the Criminal Code; enforced entry, pushing your way in; two, if they did not have a warrant, and I doubt this very much, then there was a lie and threat and, finally, there is a threat of certain action if the person did not quieten down and listen to him. Unfortunately these are three things which investigators do from time to time in complete disregard of the rights of the individual in his home or apartment, wherever he happens to be. They do these things in order to obtain evidence which would indicate that the circumstances were such that adultery may have taken place. It is unfortunate, as I say, that these things occur, but they do. I do not believe we should countenance them. I would expect that in a court of law if evidence of this nature were given of having pushed their way in, the judge might well take account of that and make some comments to the individual who gave that sort of evidence, that this was contrary to the statutes of Canada.
I would imagine, also, that the individual whose apartment this was would have cause for complaint. He could quite properly suggest that an arrest be made, on the basis of the Criminal Code, the person not having been invited into his apartment. These investigators are in an advantageous position at certain times because the individuals do not want any undue publicity given to their activities. This might result in the investigators being more forthright in their disregard of individual rights than might normally be the case. You could ask any individual in this committee if, at 10.45 in the evening, two strangers came knocking at his door and, when he went to the door they rushed in, closed the door behind them and began to ask particular questions, would he not become angry?
It is possible for these investigators to make errors from time to time and get into the wrong apartment. I had one case recounted to me in which this happened, not this particular case about which I am speaking now. The investigators made an error and broke in on somebody else, a man and his wife who were very much upset by this intrusion. I submit it is only because these investigators have an advantage that they
Private Bills-Divorce are able to get away with this sort of nonsense of pushing into an apartment. It does not matter whether it is a hotel room or an apartment, an individual rents it and has a right to privacy there. These investigators should not be allowed to barge in and violate the law in order to get some evidence. There should be some other arrangement made.
I submit that in this case, as I said earlier, primary consideration was given by the other place to the question of cruelty and to the matter of desertion. When I refer to "cruelty", I mean both mental and physical. Primary consideration was given to the fact he kept this woman almost a prisoner in his home. These were the things to which primary consideration was given by the committee of the other place. There is a reference to the husband here by one hon. senator as a bohemian or beatnik type of individual. These were the things that weighed rather heavily in the minds of the committee members of the other place in reporting favourably on this bill. Since we are not bound by any strict legislation that says adultery must be proven, these are the things that should be given the greatest amount of consideration by this committee in giving passage to this particular bill.
I should like to return to this question of the pushing in, the rushing in. I have noticed, Mr. Chairman-I hope I will be allowed to make a comment or two on this-in other instances where evidence has been given by investigators that they forced their way in, that they rifled through someone's private property such as a purse in one instance that I recall; that they engaged in thievery by taking a nameplate off a door in order to say "This is the nameplate that was on the door, so it proves that is that particular person's abode"; that they used threats in dealing with-

speechtext: It is true that the husband was a bit of a wanderer. Columbia. The only place in which the wife indicates that any support or reasonable support took place was in the province of British Columbia. At the same time I believe it has been clearly pointed out that this man lived in England, was raised in England, that his natural domicile of origin is England and that he has now returned to England. During the questioning there has been no indication that he has any intentions of returning to Canada or to the province of British Columbia or to the province of Quebec.
I think the sponsor of this bill is probably aware of the fact that domicile under the divorce laws of Canada can be established outside of the jurisdiction of the husband Which I would submit is England in this case. It can be established outside of that jurisdiction if two years have elapsed. Because of the desertion charges which are also indicated and suggested in the evidence, after two years the wife has the right by law to take the domicile of her considered residence and no longer has to come under the domicile of the husband.
This matter has been given some consideration. It not only has caused a problem where we have had to decide in Canada, for purposes of establishing domicile, that each province will be considered to be a country and that the domicile of the husband, is always the domicile of the wife whether or not she is living with the husband, even

in those cases-and this appears to be a fact in this case-where a legal separation has been granted by the court and then consideration has again been given to the marriage by the two parties and they have lived together on a number of occasions. It has been pointed out that in the case where a wife has been deserted the situation is as follows, and I am quoting from page 287 of W. Kent Power's book "The Law of Divorce in Canada":
The decision of the privy council in Cook v. Cook and Attorney General for Alberta (a) that a wife deserted by her husband cannot acquire a domicile separate from him so as to give the courts of that domicile jurisdiction to dissolve the marriage, even though she was judicially separated from him led to the enactment by the dominion parliament of the Divorce Jurisdiction Act, 1930, chapter 15, which provides:
"A married woman who either before or after the passing of the act has been deserted by and has been living separate and apart from her husband for a period of two years and upwards and is still living separate and apart from her husband, may in any one of those provinces in Canada in which there is a court having jurisdiction to grant a divorce a vinculo matrimonii, commence in the court of such province having such jurisdiction proceedings for a divorce a vinculo matrimonii praying that her marriage may be dissolved on any grounds that may entitle her to such divorce according to the law of such province and such courts shall have jurisdiction to grant such divorce provided that immediately prior to such desertion the husband of such married woman was domiciled in the province in which such proceedings are commenced."
I believe that the sponsor of this bill has an obligation to the House of Commons, and I believe he will readily admit to me that the place in which they lived together, and the only place in which they were really domiciled in the true sense of the word, was in Prince George in the province of British Columbia. It would therefore be impossible for the wife to start proceedings in the province of Quebec through the parliament of Canada when there was already recourse open to her by law in the province of British Columbia and an opportunity to get a divorce.
If the sponsor says this is not true, then I think we would have to apply our minds again to the fact that if we were to grant-* and I do not agree but I say if we were to do so-that the jurisdiction of the domicile will fall within the province of Quebec, we have still not established a separate domicile from the husband in another country, namely England. This divorce was applied for on April 17, 1959. The last time these people had met and had some discussion-and the evidence does not disclose whether or not they had a closer relationship than that-was in January, 1959, only a few months prior

to this application. If we establish the last domicile of the couple, the last time they had cohabited, the last time they had lived together as man and wife, then I think we shall have to agree that this was in the province of British Columbia and that that took place in 1958.
The law does not say that the decree can be granted two years after that. It says that two full years must go by before application is made. Quite obviously, even if we use the earliest possible date of April, 1958, we would find that we are already only in April, 1960 and that this divorce was applied for a full year ago. Hence this lady would not be eligible during that period of time to apply the Canadian divorce court act as it relates to the disallowance of marriage and she would not be able to use this as grounds for obtaining this divorce.
There are other factors in this case. I could point out that there are many problems raised in the evidence which are worthy of some consideration by the committee. I could point to the fact that there were two investigators in this case originally, that one died before he could give evidence, and therefore we have only the unsupported testimony of one investigator who in my opinion is not very reliable and has not proved to be reliable in previous cases. It is quite true we could go into all these things and discuss them at some length, but I think this is much more fundamental than a discussion of the evidence given in the Senate, namely that we are being asked to grant a divorce which in my opinion contravenes the very law passed by the house in 1930, the law of divorce in Canada.

The matter of domicile is established in several ways, but not necessarily by living in a particular province. As I understand it, you could live in any particular province. You could even make a formal declaration that you were going to live in some particular place and never establish that. There are many cases which indicate this. There is a case reported in Dicey's "Conflict of Laws", 5th (Keith's) edition, page 54 which illustrates what I mean:
With regard to the United States, an intention indefinite as to locality to live somewhere in the United States is in itself inconclusive where the question at issue is: Has A., the person whose domicile is in dispute, taken up residence in a given state with the intention of residing permanently in that state? Residing in Philadelphia with the intention, not of making his permanent home in Philadelphia, but of making his home in Philadelphia, Baltimore, or Washington, could not be effective to displace the domicile of origin.
In this particular case it has not been indicated-certainly the evidence does not indicate-that this gentleman had any intention of establishing domicile in Canada or in any particular province in Canada. He lived in the province of Quebec. He moved to the province of British Columbia and then back to the province of Quebec. Then he moved back to the United Kingdom where he was raised and had lived before, and he appears to have got a job. His wife was asked on page 8 by Senator Taylor this question:

Then, Mr. Speaker, we move on to 1959. You will, I am sure, not need to be reminded of their gloomy attitude toward the budget at that time. I think hon. members may well test the accuracy of hon. members opposite in their gloomy forecasts today by the touchstone of what they said last year with reference to last year's budget. It will be remembered that at that time, namely, April, 1959, I estimated a budget deficit for the fiscal year 1959-60 of $393 million. It recently transpired that the budget deficit was $405.6 million. I will come back later to this matter of accuracy in that respect.
But hon. members opposite were not satisfied with this; they were not satisfied at the time. They said the deficit was going to be much greater; that I had overestimated revenues; that I had taken much too optimistic a view of the economic outlook and so they said it was going to be much worse. There is the actual fact. They carried this game on all through the year. Here is my distinguished predecessor, Mr. Walter Harris, speaking quite recently. The house will recall the quotation which was read here last Friday by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) where Mr. Harris said just a month ago that "the deficit may well be $600 million." This, of course, is 50 per cent out and it just shows how far Liberals can err in their estimates when they have not the benefit of the advice of the experts that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River indicated he would fly to if he had the opportunity.
Then this afternoon we were treated to a most harrowing tale of an imminent recession by the Leader of the Opposition. He must have sent the chills up and down our spines as he pictured the horrors of this recession. It is quite clear that the Leader of the Opposition just cannot wait for the next recession to come. He is talking of it now and if he can bring it on by his talk he is certainly going to do it. He has exaggerated unemployment, just as hon. members opposite have been doing this long time, and he has created gloom so thick that he has lost his own way in it now. He is simply groping about in gloom of his own creation. There is a couplet, Mr. Speaker, from a hymn that I am sure the Leader of the Opposition must remember.
Take up the torch and wave it wide,
The torch that lights time's thickest gloom.
I commend that to the Leader of the Opposition. I hope the next time he undertakes to sing he will sing that hymn. It is No. 384 in the hymnary of the United Church.
12, 1960
The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the minister quote the next two lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, but I can quote from another hymn that speaks about "the encircling gloom". The Liberals were wrong in 1957; they were wrong in 1958; they were wrong in 1959; and they are wrong again now in 1960.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And so are you.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition was so anxious this afternoon to get everybody talking recession with him that he was in effect asking the Minister of Finance what preparations he was making for the next recession. The best preparation that can be made for the next recession is to continue the present government in office. That is the surest guarantee of avoiding a recession. I will say this to the Leader of the Opposition, that we will not find this country in the position in which it was in 1957 when the recession induced by the Liberals at that time came upon the country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We certainly will not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In one respect we can be thankful that the financial position of the government will be very much better and I mention it in passing in view of what has been said about the conversion loan by the hon. but not too well instructed members opposite. The average debt of this country will not be maturing nearly so soon, thanks to the conversion loan, as it was when we came into office in 1957.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was also being paid off when you came into office.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I come now to another subject that interests me very much, the subject of accuracy in estimating. I noted with not less than passing interest this afternoon a remark made by the Leader of the Opposition. He said: "If the minister is as far out this year as he was last year his surplus will quickly melt into a deficit". That is quite a remarkable statement to come from the hon. gentleman. It perhaps is an echo of the statement made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River as found at page 2703 of Hansard. Referring to myself he said:
Did he get discouraged from the poor estimating that was done last year?
Let us examine the estimating that was done last year in the light of the figures as we have them at the present time. They are not complete, but they are estimates that were made as of the last week of March. I have reminded the house that the deficit estimated by me in the budget of April, 1959 was $393 million. It proved to be $405.6

The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming million, an increase of $12.6 million or a little less than 3 per cent over the estimate.
Is this a departure that indicates inaccuracy in budgeting, that calls for the kind of comment that was made by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon or the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River a week ago yesterday? Evidently the Ottawa Citizen does not think so, for in an editorial which appeared on March 31, the day that the white paper was tabled in the house, I read the following with reference to the figure of $405.6 million:
The figure is higher than Mr. Fleming thought it would be when he made his budget forecast last April ($393 million) but it is not far out as these matters are measured.
That is an interesting comment. I ask hon. members opposite to consider what was the estimate and what it was based on. In the budget speech of April 9, 1959 this is what I said about the basis of the estimate, as found at page 2409 of Hansard:
-I shall be basing my budgetary policy and my revenue forecasts on a gross national product of about $34J billion which is about 7 per cent above the average level achieved in 1958.
Hon. members opposite have been laying great stress on the 7 per cent. They have been saying latterly, "Oh, but the figures now show it was only 6 per cent". I have a comment to make upon that. Let me remind the house that I based my budget estimate on the forecast of a gross national product of $34| billion. I commented that that was 7 per cent above 1958. We actually reached a figure of about $34.6 billion instead of a figure of $34.5 billion. When the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River referred to this forecast in speaking in the house a week ago yesterday he did not say anything about the $34.5 billion. He took half the sentence and he chose the half with a view to leaving out the figure. He simply said that I had based the budget forecast on the view that the gross national product in 1959 would show an increase of 7 per cent over 1958. As it turned out we exceeded in gross national product the figure on which I based the budget forecast.
But that turned out to be only an increase of 6 per cent over 1958. And why? When hon. members opposite use this figure they ought to be frank enough or informed enough to tell the whole story and to give it to the house. The fact is that the figure calculated on the 1958 gross national product was advanced during the year by the dominion bureau of statistics. There was a change in the calculation and it was the 1958 figure that was advanced. The 1959 forecast was reached; indeed, it was slightly passed. It


was the change of the 1958 figure that accounts for the fact that the increase was only
6	per cent instead of 7 per cent over 1958. That did not affect the forecast, as the figures have shown.
But let me not dwell unduly on that. Let me turn now to what the opposition had to say about the increase in the gross national product for 1959 over 1958 when they were engaged in the budget debate a year ago. Here is the Leader of the Opposition speaking on April 21 last year, as found at page 2912 of Hansard. He referred to my forecast of $34.5 billion or a 7 per cent increase and he continued:
He made no attempt then to justify this optimistic forecast, and he made no attempt to justify it this afternoon. It is a forecast which has been dismissed by many experts, and I will name mine, although he did not name his this afternoon. They include the Canadian tax foundation, the financial editor of the Montreal Gazette, and indeed the Canadian chamber of commerce, which in its submission to the government forecast a gross physical output in 1959-60 of approximately 1 per cent, not
7	per cent.
That was the forecast of the Leader of the Opposition and I suggest that his forecast today and his comments on the forecast upon which the 1960 budget is based can well be judged in the light of his errors as revealed a year ago in the budget debate. But his characteristic pessimism in opposition did not end there. He went on to say at page 2913:
My calculations on this point last year, as stated in my budget speech, were that the minister was too optimistic.
"Too optimistic", that has been their cry. Further down in the paragraph he said:
He does not give us any basis for his optimism.
I am content to have the 1959 budget forecast judged in the light of events. I do not think you can get any better or more searching test than that. I am quite prepared to have my forecast tested by the facts. I do not think the Leader of the Opposition would wish to have his tested by the facts. He had the temerity this afternoon to say in one of the more extraordinary statements in his speech, that his predictions last year have been borne out by the events.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sure, they have.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We will not expect too much from the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud). If 7 per cent and 1 per cent are the same thing to him, I do not think any of us can do very much to help the hon. member. The Leader of the Opposition poured scorn on our forecasts last year, but I think they have been borne out by the facts. Let us not judge these hon. gentlemen opposite by their despondency in these days in opposition. Let us go back

and judge the accuracy of the forecasting and budgeting that has been done for the last three budgets as contrasted with the period when the Liberals were in office. I do not want to take the house back over the whole record, so let us start with the postwar period.
Let us start with the fiscal year 1946-47. In that year, they forecast a deficit of $300 million, and they were just out $674 million in that estimate. There was an error of 22.4 per cent in the revenue forecast and 25.6 per cent on expenditures. I am prepared to make allowances for that year because it was the first full fiscal year of peace. I expect it was a very difficult year in which to make forecasts. I am prepared to make allowances for that year. Let us go on to 1947-48. They forecast a surplus of $190 million and they finished up with $676 million, for a difference of $486 million. In 1948-49 they were out by $107 million; in 1949-50, they were out $47 million; in 1950-51, they were out $196 million. So it goes, on down the line. I do not know whether or not hon. members can stand much more of this. If you want something in the way of a comparison, go back to these figures in past Liberal regimes. You can check the margin of difference between the actual figures and the figures forecast.
If hon. members want more of this I can say that in 1950-51 the difference was $196 million; 1951-52, $218 million; 1952-53, they were close that year, $15 million; 1953-54, $35 million; 1954-55, $156 million; 1955-56, $127 million, and 1956-57, $145 million. Yet they talk about inaccuracies in my budgeting.
The Leader of the Opposition says that if the present minister is as far out this year as he was last year his surplus will quickly melt into a deficit. All I can say is that we have budgeted carefully. We have made the most careful forecasts that we can, and I would not have submitted this budget to the house had I not believed it is an honest, straightforward budget that will stand up to the test of the best estimating possible at the date on which the budget was introduced.
I will come back to say some things about this matter of records. We were told this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition and we have been told by others, that, after all, this surplus of $12 million that has been forecast is nothing. Apparently it was not even worth announcing in the house in the view of hon. members opposite. The $12 million does not hold the record, even in recent years, for the smallest forecast of a deficit or the smallest forecast of a surplus. I am sure hon. members opposite will be glad to have their faltering memories
12, 1960
The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming refreshed if I recall to them that in the fiscal year 1954-55, the last budget of Mr. Abbott, now Mr. Justice Abbott, he forecast a surplus of $4 million. Did hon. members opposite rise in holy horror and say, this is too small; this should not even be announced? No, they came forward then and said it was an honest estimate.
I might just mention in passing what happened that year. Perhaps it was this experience that gave rise to some of the cynical comments by hon. members opposite as to what might happen this year. In place of that forecast surplus of $4 million, at the end of the year there was a Liberal deficit of $152 million.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This was not the
only year in which a small surplus was forecast. In the previous year, 1953-54, the surplus forecast at the time of the budget was $11 million; in 1952-53 it was $9 million forecast in the budget; in 1950-51, $20 million, later changed to $15 million. So let it not be said that this 1960 surplus is the albino of its breed. There are numerous precedents for a forecast of a relatively small surplus.
I may say that the comments by the Leader of the Opposition on the forecast surplus have been interesting. He is reported in a Canadian Press dispatch of April 2 as having said in Toronto that my budget will have to be tested by time. That was a profound statement indeed. I had thought that every budget had to be tested by time. I hope my budget will be tested by time and not by the vagaries, errors and caprices of hon. members opposite.
Before we leave this subject of the derision that they have heaped on this budget surplus of $12 million, let me say this, and I address my comment particularly to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. He wanted to add to the 1959-60 deficit the deficit in the old age security account. It will be interesting to see what the hon. gentleman will say next year in the budget debate when that old age security account shows, as we expect it will, a surplus on next year's operation of perhaps $40 million. I am sure he will be the first to come forward and say, I insist on adding the $40 million to the announced budget surplus, as announced by the Minister of Finance in the white paper.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Because you have added taxes of millions and millions of dollars last year for this account.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Apparently the hon. member cannot keep his seat. There must be something contagious in that seat over there.

The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming It was his seatmate the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate this afternoon, and I suppose these things spread.
We were told this afternoon that there are some surpluses that are good. There is virtue in some surpluses, but not the Conservative kind. We were told that in times past the Conservatives had not approved of surpluses. This is poppycock.
Our quarrel with the surpluses in the days of easy financing in the post-war period before this Liberal induced recession was that they did not budget properly and they did not plan for debt retirement. It was always on a hit and miss basis, and the surpluses were not those for which they budgeted. The budgeting was inaccurate in many of those years. Never once did they set out at the first of the year to make plans for debt retirement. It was always catch as catch can. Never was there any planning in that respect. Having heard the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon talk about orderly debt reduction and say that they look back to orderly debt reduction on the part of the Liberal administration, may I just say this. He is looking back and he is seeing things that just are not there. One can understand why there is nothing for him to look forward to.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, always.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the minister really think it is a really terrible thing to pay off a little bit more of the national debt than you thought at the beginning of the year you were going to be able to pay off?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, but I like to see these things done in an orderly and planned way and not the arrival at surpluses at the end of the year by errors and consequent over-taxation. That was where the over-taxation occurred, namely because the country was not being given proper budgeting.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are taking a billion dollars more than the Liberals took in 1956-57.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Where we are quarrelling with hon. members opposite is that they never planned for any orderly debt reduction at all. They are simply seeing things now that did not occur at all.
I wish to pass on from these agitated and garrulous gentlemen to talk about the subject of muddle. They have been talking lately about the muddle. Unquestionably there is a muddle but it is not where they think it is. The fact is that they are so muddled and befuddled that they think everybody else is


muddled and befuddled because they are. This is a psychopathic situation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has the time not come for the minister to discuss the serious business of the nation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What was that
remark?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was just saying this to my hon. and dear friend. Does he not think, as Minister of Finance, that the time has come in this house when he should discuss the serious business of the nation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have been-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. If I might interject here, I should like to say that it seems to me that far too many bright thoughts are being expressed at the wrong time tonight and that it would be better if the house would give to the minister who has the floor the full use of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have been discussing what hon. members opposite have been saying in the course of this debate. By the definition applied by the hon. member for Essex East apparently what they have said was not serious business of the country.
Hon. members opposite have been completely, utterly and hopelessly self-confused. In the course of this debate we have seen on their part confusion thrice confounded. We do not know yet whether these hon. gentlemen advocate today a balanced budget or a deficit. They have all had ample opportunity to speak in the course of this debate. The Leader of the Opposition left us in a complete quandary on this subject at the end of his remarks today. He was on both sides of the question. Indeed, he was on both sides of every question that he allowed himself to touch upon in his remarks today.
It remains an unresolved mystery as to whether the official opposition in this situation believes that the government should budget for a balanced budget or a deficit. To use an expression that was coined by a president of the United States about 50 years aeo, to try to get some sense and some clear expression of opinion from the Liberals on 'his question you might just as well try to nail jelly to the wall. We have witnessed on their part hopeless floundering or else calculated double-talk. We thought the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon was going to come close to saying something. But having reached the point where it seemed that he was coming close, he backed away and went off on a tangent. What did he say? This is what he said this afternoon. He said that today no

government should be afraid of a deficit if related to a plan and not due to un-co-ji'dinated circumstances.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is not all of
it; that is not the whole sentence.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is just half the
sentence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was as much as I was able to take down; and believe me, of the sentence uttered by the Leader of the Opposition, this is much the better part.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Dishonest as usual.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He said that today no government should be afraid of a deficit. Did he mean to convey the idea that he was advocating a deficit? Is that what he meant?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He was talking about social need. I am surprised at my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He sits in the front pew of a church and then says this kind of thing.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. If hon. members have views to express they might at least rise in their places.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition, having permitted himself to say that today no government should be afraid of a deficit-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. You have asked us to rise and I think you are quite right in giving that direction. This is the third time in the last half minute the Minister of Finance has misquoted the statement of the Leader of the Opposition. The Leader of the Opposi-sion related deficit to the problem of social need-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And depression.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -and the possibility of depression and further recession. The Minister of Finance has misquoted the words of the Leader of the Opposition in a shameful manner.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps the correction might more appropriately have been made at the end of the minister's speech. Will the minister proceed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think the house will have taken note-and everybody is glad to see it-that the hon. member for Essex East is laughing and snickering at himself now. He does not laugh at his interventions half as much as do the rest of us in this house.
12, 1960
The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming
I compliment the hon. member for Essex East on having greatly improved the speech made this afternoon in this respect by the Leader of the Opposition. That is what the Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon about a deficit.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He did not say
that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have his words here. I trust my note of them much better than I trust the failing memory of the hon. member for Essex East unless he was the man who wrote the speech of the Leader of the Opposition. He said that today no government should be afraid of a deficit-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is half of the sentence and the minister knows it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Here is the rest of it; if related to a plan and not due to un-co-ordinated something or other.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not correct. This is a thoroughly dishonest performance.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Withdraw.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I know the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would be the first to object to an interjection of that kind and I hope he will make the proper correction.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I quite
deliberately said that was a thoroughly dishonest performance and it is my opinion that it was a thoroughly dishonest performance. I listened carefully to what the Leader of the Opposition said. What he said was that if we had a real depression, a government should not be afraid of a deficit. If the Minister of Finance was not listening carefully he should not quote half a sentence. I give the minister credit for not having been deliberately misquoting the Leader of the Opposition because he has said that he did not hear it all. But when he says he did not hear it all it seems to me it is a dishonest performance to treat it as though it were a full sentence.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Withdraw.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not sure whether I understood the hon. member. I thought he began by withdrawing the words "dishonest performance" because in my view "dishonest performance" means a deliberately untrue statement. The hon. member knows that it is not permissible, within the standards of debate which we set for ourselves, to impute deliberate untruth and dishonesty to another hon. member.

The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think you will agree I have always respected your rulings. If there is any imputation that I suggested that the Minister of Finance was deliberately dishonest-although I think he was carelessly dishonest-if the word "dishonest" should not be used I will say he was shockingly misleading.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask for an unconditional withdrawal of the word "dishonest".

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I understand the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has unreservedly withdrawn the word "dishonest".

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, quite; I have unreservedly withdrawn the word "dishonest".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then we are making progress, Mr. Speaker. I wonder how much more the hon. member feels like withdrawing.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Order. If hon. members
would allow the minister to proceed I am sure the debate would be more progressive.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister should not provoke us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sorry to be provoking to the hon. member. Believe me, nothing is further from my thoughts than that I should be provoking to the hon. member for Essex East.
In asking ourselves about this muddle on the part of hon. members opposite and where they stand on the question of a deficit or a balanced budget, I recall that in 1958 they attacked our planned deficit. In 1959 they attacked our planned deficit. In 1960 they went back and re-attacked the deficits we had had in 1958 and 1959. And now also, Mr. Speaker, in 1960 they have attacked our balanced budget for 1960-61. Where is the sense in all of this and where is the consistency? These hon. members are in a muddle and are just wildly attacking everything which the government puts forward; that is the explanation.
Here again I recall what the Leader of the Opposition said in his Toronto speech of April 2. This Canadian Press dispatch says:
While admitting the government's balanced budget might be all to the good-
Did we hear him say that this afternoon? Did we hear him say that the government's balanced budget might be all to the good? No, Mr. Speaker; no one opposite has even admitted that this balanced budget might be all to the good. I have marvelled at some parliamentary performances, but I think Houdini in his best and palmiest days might

well have envied this rubber-jointed, double-jointed performance on the part of sleight of hand artists opposite.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What are you reading from?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Something you would not understand; it is plain English. It is because they are in this horrible muddle and do not know where they are going that they keep on contradicting themselves.
I spoke of their position in times past. In 1958 they were advocating or having good words to say about the idea of budget deficits. On January 19, 1959, as reported on page 35 of Hansard, the Leader of the Opposition said:
The previous administration did not hesitate to budget for a deficit when there was a threat of recession.
Apparently it was all right for them to do it, but it was not all right for us to budget for a deficit in 1958 and 1959, coping in the first year with recession and in the second year with the continuing effects.
I will defend, as I have defended before, the measures that led us into deficit financing in 1958 and 1959. We coped with that recession and spent money to increase the social security payments in this country, and in that way we increased consumer purchasing. We spent a good deal of money to stimulate housing, and not only helped the housing situation but as well reduced unemployment very greatly. The hon. member is most gracious.
I have reminded the house of the resolutions that relate to tariff proposals and how they affect the textile trade in certain regards. This leads me to make a comment concerning our trade relations with Japan. Attempts have been made on the part of hon. members opposite, not in a very straightforward way, more by stealth than otherwise, to make a political football out of this question. Let me make it as clear as I can that we in the government will do all we reasonably can to avoid matters pertaining to Japanese trade becoming a political football in this country.
Our relations with Japan are very friendly. We desire a valuable two-way commercial relationship in our trade with Japan. I pointed out before that our desire is for trade growth on an orderly basis. Orderly growth is the feature of the trade policy we pursue with respect to Japan. Our position in this respect has been brutally misrepresented, particularly in western Canada. Papers like the Winnipeg Free Press and the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix have been seeking to mislead western Canada into thinking that the policy of the federal government is somehow going to hurt the Japanese market for Canadian wheat and other products. There is not and there never was any foundation in fact for that attempt to mislead the people of western Canada. This has been misrepresentation.


I can cite some facts in this regard and I shall do so; but let me first of all comment on the fact that export quotas are applied by Japan with respect to shipments of certain commodities to Canada. Where did the system of export quotas originate, and when? Let us have an end to the double-talk from hon. members opposite. Those quotas originated in the time of the Liberal government in this country. The quota on cotton blouses and sportshirts was applied January 1, 1956; the quota on cotton fabrics, on April 1, 1956; the quota on cotton damask table cloths applied September 1, 1956; the quota on cotton coats and slacks, February 1, 1957; the quota on cotton knitted wear, February 1, 1957; the quota on cotton pillow cases, February 1, 1957. Now, when we are negotiating the application of quotas for 1960 on this and on spun rayon and other products you would think we were throwing to the winds all concern for the export markets of western Canada in Japan. Did you ever hear anything more hypocritical than hon. members opposite who were the authors of most of the system of export quotas applied by Japan in its shipments to Canada? The story does not end there.
The trade of these two countries is carried on in pursuance of an agreement that was entered into between these two countries in 1954. I do not need to remind you what party was in power in Canada in 1954. I may remind you that the Japanese trade treaty was fully supported by the Conservative party in this house in the debate on this measure in 1954. That trade agreement was accompanied by an exchange of letters, and a letter written on March 31, 1954 to the ambassador of Japan to Canada contains this statement:
On the occasion of signing the agreement on commerce between Canada and Japan, I have the honour to inform Your Excellency that the government of Canada reserves the right to establish values for ordinary and special duty purposes in the following terms:
1.	If, as a result of unforeseen developments and of the effect of the obligations incurred by Canada under the aforesaid agreement, any product is being imported into its territory in such increased quantities and under such conditions as to cause or threaten serious injury to the domestic producers in its territory of like or directly competitive products, Canada will be free, in respect of such product, and to the extent and for such a time as may be necessary to prevent or remedy such injury, to establish values for ordinary and special duty purposes.
2.	In determining whether values should be established in respect of any product pursuant to paragraph 1 and in determining the level at which such values should be established, Canada will take into account the prices of like or directly competitive products, if any, being imported at that time from other countries.
3.	Before Canada takes action pursuant to paragraph I, it will give notice in writing to Japan as

far in advance as may be practicable and will afford the latter an opportunity to consult with it in respect of the proposed action. In critical circumstances, where delay would cause damage which it would be difficult to repair, action under paragraph 1 may be taken provisionally without prior consultation, on the condition that consultation shall take place immediately after taking such action.
Perhaps I should read the balance of the letter. There is only a paragraph.
I have the honour to state further that in the view of the government of Canada these provisions are consistent with the general agreement on tariffs and trade and that the government of Canada will regard these provisions as continuing to be applicable in the event that the general agreement on tariffs and trade is applied between Canada and Japan.
That is a letter written on March 31, 1954, a letter that stipulated the right on the part of Canada to apply fixed values for duty, special values for duty, on Japanese imports into Canada where there was a threat of serious injury to domestic producers in Canada as a result of imports in increased quantities. Do you know who signed that letter, Mr. Speaker? Who set up the provision in this regard that gives Canada the right to impose fixed values for duty on imports from Japan under this treaty? Oh, Mr. Speaker, think of it. The name appended to this letter is L. B. Pearson, secretary of state for external affairs.

It just gives the answer to the nonsense or exposes the nonsense talked by hon. members opposite.
I have made no apology for what I have said to the house concerning the reasons for confidence in the Canadian outlook. I do not share at all the gloomy statements which were made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition. He did not give a fair, a balanced picture in what he said about our current accounts balance of payments.
As I tried to follow him this afternoon I think he was speaking about 1956, and he said the balance against us was $1.2 billion. He left the impression, as I understood his remarks, that this applied to all transactions and he said that today the balance of payments deficit was increasing. However, if I correctly apprehended his remarks, the Leader of the Opposition is quite wrong. Let me give him the figures for 1956 in relation to our current balance of payments deficit with the United States. In 1956, the last full calendar year of Liberal rule, the deficit in our merchandise trade with the United States was $1,167 million; our deficit on nonmerchandise items was $472 million in that year; our deficit on both accounts with the United States was $1,639 million. He left the impression that this condition was growing worse, so I lay alongside those figures the figures for 1959 in relation to our balance of payments with the United States. In 1959 the merchandise balance deficit was $518 million and the non-merchandise deficit totalled $718 million, a total of $1,236 million. This represents an improvement by way of reduction in the deficit in our commercial relations with the United States between those two years of $403 million. This just accidentally escaped the attention of the Leader of the Opposition.
In so far as the extraordinary statements he made this afternoon about the actions of the Bank of Canada in relation to the purchase and sale of bonds are concerned, either the Leader of the Opposition did not understand the situation at all or he was proceeding on quite erroneous information. I do not direct the operations of the Bank of Canada in relation to its purchases and sales of bonds. The Minister of Finance has no authority to do that. The bank reaches its own decisions in that respect. Indeed, while they may occasionally acquaint the minister with what they are doing in that respect or what they are aiming to do, they do not consult him in relation to their own decisions in this respect. He has no authority over them in that regard. When reference is made to the fact that the Bank of Canada has been selling long term bonds, then apparently the Leader of the

Opposition is not aware that this has the effect of increasing the yields of long term bonds and widening the spread between long term and short term interest rates; that this, in turn, has the effect of stimulating saving by giving more incentive to investors to hold long term bonds. In its operations, I think the Bank of Canada has been proceeding in a way very different from that described to the house this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition.
In my concluding remarks, let me say this: There is a sound basis for confidence in Canada today. All the gloom that the Leader of the Opposition and his associates are creating, if people would listen to them, is not going to change the facts and these are facts that give reason for solid confidence in Canada.
Let me remind the house very quickly that, in the first place, inflation has been contained. As I said in the budget speech, many of the inflationary factors are quiescent. We cannot rest on our laurels, however. We have to be vigilant in this respect at all times. It is well, however, to proceed on facts, not on errors, as hon. members opposite have been doing. They would have you believe that we have not been successful in our efforts to grapple with inflation.
Here are the figures. The consumer price index in January, 1959, was 126.1 and in March, 1960, 126.9. Does that sound as though things got out of hand in 1959? Here is what the Leader of the Opposition said a year ago in his doleful prophecy about inflation. According to page 2914 of Hansard for April 21, 1959, he said this:
This year there should be less, but still serious, unemployment and a greater danger of inflation.
How wrong can he be? Here are the figures for the general index of wholesale prices. In January, 1959, it was 229.7 and in March, 1960, 229.6. Does that sound as though inflation got out of hand in 1959? These are the facts, and the incontestable facts.
Next, in speaking of trade, I have pointed to the fact that in 1959 Canada's export trade reached an all time record of $5.2 billion, and the rapid increase has continued in 1960. In the first two months of 1960 domestic exports of this country reached a total of $832 million as compared with $655 million in the same two months a year ago. This represents an increase of approximately one third in our exports in the first two months of this year over the first two months of last year. What shall we say of the hon. member for Essex East who, according to the press, used this expression in Montreal on April 6: "The stagnation in Canada's export trade".
12, 1960
The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming We have apparently an all time record, with rapid increases, but to the hon. member for Essex East this means stagnation.
Hon. members are now aware of the decision that was announced last week in relation to the export of gas and what this is going to mean in terms of the expansion of the Canadian economy and again in contributing to a better balance in our commercial relations with the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This decision was reached after having satisfied ourselves by an exhaustive inquiry that the needs of Canadians would first be assured.

After having satisfied
yourself that C. D. Howe was right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The last point to which I have time to refer is the fact that benefits have already accrued to the Canadian economy from this balanced budget. The fact is that it has brought renewed confidence to the Canadian people and to the Canadian economy. In the budget speech I said that it is going to make it easier for the provinces, the municipalities and business to borrow in Canada because the federal government will be largely withdrawing from the role of a net borrower. Already benefits have been experienced in this regard. One has only to look at the reception accorded to a recent province of Ontario bond issue at a lower rate of interest than that at which they were borrowing quite recently.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You promised that two years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You see this renewed confidence expressed in that way. There are other benefits that are going to follow from the budget and from this withdrawal of the federal government from a net borrowing position. There will be less occasion than there was-if indeed there was any justification-for provinces and municipalities to be going to the United States to borrow, with all the dangers in that respect of which I have attempted respectfully to give warning. Already we are seeing benefits in this respect. It is only about a month ago that the premium on the Canadian dollar was five cents. Today it is less than three and a half cents.
